title: Week 3
text:
The Coefficients
The coefficients are displayed in the results as follows:



Coefficients


The values of these coefficients determine the shape of the s-shaped curve we derived above. Strictly speaking, the slope coefficient determines the steepness of the curve, and the intercept determines its horizontal position. To see exactly how different values of the intercept (\(\beta_0\)) and the slope (\(\beta_1\)) coefficients affect the curve, please use the application below (it may take a moment to load, as it is a web-based application).

  Open Application      

But how do we interpret the coefficients substantively? As you have seen in the Theory section above, the relationship between our independent variable and the probability of democracy is not linear: the curve was s-shaped, so that the increment in probability is not the same for, say moving from \(x_{1}\) to \(x_{2}\) and from \(x_{2}\) to \(x_{3}\). For illustration see the orange bars in the following Figure:
   






Figure 6: Marginal Effects for Life Expectancy on the Probability of Democracy



   
What we therefore need to do in the world of probit, is to evaluate the probability at individual values of \(x_{i}\), or put differently, assess how much of the bell-shaped curve has slid across our cut-off point \(\tau\) (tau) at a particular point \(x_{i}\). And this brings us to predicted probabilities.

title: Week 3
text:
Predicted Probabilities
Once we have estimated the model, we have determined the shape of the s-shaped curve in Figure 4. What we now need to do, is to evaluate the probability on the y-axis for different values on the x-axis. In our case this is the variable life.

Setting the x-values
Let us first get a basic overview of the variable life. We can do this by calling

summary(world2000$life)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
  44.83   60.63   69.58   66.79   73.96   82.12       4 


So we know that the average life expectancy in the world in the year 2000 was 66.79 years, with a minimum of 44.83 years, and a maximum of 82.12 years. We also have 4 missing observations (NA) which we need to exclude from the following by setting na.rm=TRUE2, as R is otherwise unable to calculate descriptive measures within the setx function, such as the mean. Let us set life to its mean now, by typing:

setx = data.frame(life=66.70)

If you want to change this value for calculations later on, you simply set different values in the setx dataframe or specify a new one).
We now have the shape of the probability curve, and we have agreed on a point on the x-axis. We are finally ready to have a look at the probability to be a democracy at this point.


Predicting the Probability
The quantity of interest we are interested in is the probability of being a democracy. To calculate this quantity of interest, we use the function predict() and specify within this function for which model we want to calculate the quantity, and the data frame in which we specified the value of our x-variable. In our case this variable is life and we have assigned the mean value to an object called setx earlier.

predict(probit, setx, type="response")

        1 
0.5582287 


Remember that we have put the value of life expectancy at the mean. For this level of life expectancy R returns to us a probability of being a democracy at 55.82%. Contrarily, this means that probability to be an autocracy is 44.18% (the two probabilities always sum up to 1).
Now we set life expectancy to its minimum

setx = data.frame(life=min(world2000$life, na.rm = T))

and calculate the quantity of interest again. Our probabilities have changed very drastically (ensure you get the same results before proceeding):

predict(probit, setx, type="response")

        1 
0.1262815 


If we set life expectancy to its maximum (how?), then we receive the following regime probabilities:

predict(probit, setx, type="response")

        1 
0.8546744 


Now we can make statements such as:

In 2000, a country’s probability to be a democracy with average life expectancy was 55.82%.
At the minimum life expectancy of 44.83 years, this probability drops by 43.19 percentage points to 12.63%.
As such, a country in 2000 at minimum life expectancy would more likely be an autocracy than a democracy (why?).



All Predicted Probabilities
It is also possible to depict the predicted probabilities for all values of your independent graphically. That would look like this:
   






Figure 7: Predicted Probabilities



   



Code for the Predicted Probabilities Graph


probit <- glm(democracy ~ life, 
               family = binomial(link = "probit"), 
               data = world2000)

xlife <- seq(0, 81.08, 1)

ylife <- predict(probit, list(life = xlife),type="response")

predictions <- data.frame(xlife,ylife) 

ggplot(data=predictions, aes(x=xlife, y=ylife)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x= "Life Expectancy at Birth", y="Pr(Democracy)") +
  theme_classic()+
  theme(axis.text=element_text(size=14),
        axis.title=element_text(size=16))

title: Week 3
text:
How to Report Results
The question is now: how do you report all of this in an article, or closer to home, in your assessment? Let us start by calculating a model which assesses the impact of per capita GDP on the probability to be a democracy in 2000, worldwide. The R commands and output look like this:

probit1 <- glm(democracy ~ gdppc,
                data = world2000,

You see, this table manages to convey clearly the relationship we are assessing, the label of the independent variable (not in the form of cryptic variable names), the value of the intercept, the value of the slope coefficient, their respective p-value, and the number of observations. It also has an informative caption underneath and is properly labelled (so that it can be cross-referenced in the text). As such, the table itself could already communicate the main take-away message without somebody looking at the text. This needs to be the goal: the table, or figure needs to be able to communicate the message without having to look at the text. In turn, the text needs to be able to communicate the message on its own without looking at the table. But both need to say the same thing.
After you have reported the results of the regression output in this way, you can then proceed to interpret (in the text) the transition probabilities as discussed above. Again, you might wish to sum up the main results in tabular format.

modelsummary
Rather than setting tables manually in Excel, or even worse in Word (it basically violates all standards of professional table formatting), you can let R do this work for you. All you need for this is the modelsummary package (Arel-Bundock, 2022).
Just like writing a shopping list, we start by creating a list of models for which we want modelsummary to produce a table. You can merely list the names of the objects in which the models are stored, such as probit1, or you can give them specific names which will appear as column titles in the table. This addition is by no means a must, but sometimes you might wish to give models a particular name, for example if you have used different methods of estimation, different components of a theory, emergence vs. survival, etc. By default, modelsummary just numbers models in ascending order.

models <- list(
  "(1)"    = probit1
)

This simple step is already sufficient to produce – an admittedly somewhat crude – results table. All we have to do is to load the modelsummary package and to use the previously defined list of models as the argument of the modelsummary() function:

library(modelsummary)
modelsummary(models)


Execute these code chunks as we go through this Section, so you can see the alterations we make to the table in real-time.

This table is a vast improvement on the raw R output you would receive when calling summary(model1). But it is far from finished. One characteristic which is conspicuously absent is an assessment of statistical significance. In model summaries of this kind this information is usually provided in the form of asterisks or other symbols next to the respective coefficient. We can add these simply by adding the option stars=TRUE to the code.

modelsummary(models,
             stars = TRUE)

Next up is the modification of the stub. The stub is the leftmost column in which you name the indicators for which coefficients will be presented. In the stub, “[a]bbreviate nothing. And never ever ever use computer variable names to stand for concepts. These are personal code words that convey no meaning to readers.” (Stimson, n.d., p. 10) Following this advice, let us add proper labels to the independent variables.
To let modelsummary know how to replace each variable name, we create a so-called coefficient map. This is really just a character vector which follows a “before-after” logic in each of its rows. For example 'gddpc'='per capita GDP' replaces the variable name gdppc with the label per capita GDP. We need to do this for all the variables we used in our models. I am storing this in a vector called cm which stands for coefficient map.

cm <- c('gdppc'    = 'per capita GDP',
        '(Intercept)' = 'Intercept')

The next step is easy, as we only need to feed this coefficient map into the modelsummary code with the option coef_map=cm:

modelsummary(models,
             stars = TRUE,
             coef_map = cm)

This is a personal thing, but I also like to show the label of the dependent variable in results tables. They just feel incomplete to me without this information. There is no default to achieve this in modelsummary and so we need to use a little trick.
What I want to add in the first row, but only in the second columm, is the text “Dependent Variable: Democracy”. This requires us to alter the style of the table slightly. modelsummary uses another package called tinytable to style the output. We load the package with library(tinytable) and instruct R to place the text where we want it.

library(tinytable)
modelsummary(models,
             stars = TRUE,
             coef_map = cm)|>
  group_tt(j = list("Dependent Variable: Democracy" = 2))

Lastly, let us tackle the model fit statistics. By default, modelsummary prints a whole festival of these into the bottom section of the table, but I want to concentrate only on the number of observations for now. We will be adding a model fit measure in Week 7.

modelsummary(models,
             stars = TRUE,
             coef_map = cm,
             gof_omit = 'DF|Deviance|Log.Lik|F|AIC|BIC|RMSE')|>
  group_tt(j = list("Dependent Variable: Democracy" = 2))

It is worth investing some time into this. There is a learning curve at the beginning, but it will make your life so much easier further down the line.


Multiple Independent Variables
As in multiple linear regression, you can also have multiple independent variables in a probit model. Schematically this would look as follows:

probit <- glm(depvar ~ indepvar1 + indepvar2 + indepvar3, 
              data = dataframe, 
              family = binomial(link = "probit"))

The fun starts when you begin to calculate probabilities for different values for all of these independent variables.

Setting the x-values
You can set the value for each variable individually, such as in this little example:

setx = data.frame(gdppc=min(world2000$gdppc, na.rm = T),
                  life=66.49)




Predicting the Probability
This is very much the same as above with one independent variable. It is crucial to remember which variables you have set at which value, so that you can interpret the probability values correctly. As in linear regression, the interpretation of individual variables is ceteris paribus. It therefore makes sense, if you wish to isolate the effect of one, single variable, only to vary the values of that variable, and to leave all the other ones the same. If you varied two variables at the same time, for example, you would no doubt see a change in probability, but you could not attribute it to a single independent variable, any more.

title: Week 3
text:
Limitations
Just as with OLS, the probit model in the form presented here works only for cross-sectional data. We have estimated the probability of being a democracy in a single year, the year 2000, treating each country as an independent observation. But the questions we ultimately care about – when and why democracies emerge, and when and why they collapse – are inherently about change over time, and that means time-series data.
The reason is directly analogous to the rationale we encountered with OLS last week. There, the problem was that the error terms in time-series data are rarely independent of one another: a country’s democracy score this year is not independent of its score last year, so the unmeasured factors lurking in the error term persist across years, producing autocorrelation. Probit faces exactly the same difficulty. Whether a country is a democracy in 2010 is plainly not independent of whether it was a democracy in 2009: regimes are sticky, and whatever unobserved forces sustained democracy in one year are very likely still at work the next. Treating repeated observations on the same country as if they came from entirely separate entities ignores this dependence, and our standard errors – and therefore our p-values – can no longer be trusted.
Therefore, we will need to make some alterations to the estimation process, before you can model the emergence and survival of democracies in your assessment – stay tuned!

Transferring this to Probit
How would all of this look in the world of probit? Let’s bring the example back to the purpose of the module, and look at how per capita GDP and the share of natural resource rents affect a country’s probability to be a democracy. The setup is analogous to the linear case, but interpretation changes in one important way: as we established last week, the coefficients live on the latent index scale, not the probability scale. To illustrate, let’s make democracy the dependent variable and ask how GDP per capita relates to it, and whether that relationship depends on resource dependence:

probit6 <- glm(democracy ~ log.gdppc * resource_state,
               data = world, family = binomial(link = "probit"))

So here is Table 2 translated into the binary world:
 



Table 7: Interpreting Interaction Coefficients (Probit)










Coefficient
Label
Interpretation




\(\beta_1\)
Logged GDP per capita
In Low-Resource states (the reference category), a one-unit increase in logged GDP per capita slides a country \(\beta_1 = 0.462\) along the \(\Phi\) curve. The sign gives the direction — a positive value pushes a country towards democracy, a negative one away from it. But because this is a position on the curve rather than a probability, how large a change in the probability of democracy it produces depends on where the country already sits: a lot in the steep middle, very little out in the flat tails.


\(\beta_2\)
High Resources
This coefficient is insignificant, so we cannot interpret it substantively; but for illustration, suppose it were. At \(\log(\text{GDP})=0\), being a High-Resource rather than a Low-Resource state shifts a country’s place on the \(\Phi\) curve by \(\beta_2 = 2.184\). Translated into a probability, the difference in the probability of being a democracy is \(\Phi(\beta_0+\beta_2)-\Phi(\beta_0) = 0.153\) (≈ 15.3 pp). This is evaluated at \(\log(\text{GDP})=0\) — a GDP per capita of $1, far outside the data — so treat it as a mechanical reference point, and remember the gap is not constant across GDP levels.


\(\beta_3\)
Logged GDP \(\times\) High Resources
\(\beta_3 = -0.366\) tells us how much more or less a one-unit increase in logged GDP moves a country along the latent probit index when it is a High-Resource rather than a Low-Resource state. Crucially, this is not the interaction effect on the probability of being a democracy. Because the same movement along the \(\Phi\) curve can imply different probability changes depending on where a country starts, the interaction measured in actual probabilities can be sizeable even when \(\beta_3\) is near zero — and can even have the opposite sign. We therefore should not read the probability-scale interaction directly from \(\beta_3\); instead, we recover it from predicted probabilities or marginal effects (see Ai & Norton, 2003).






 
You know from last week that in a probit model the coefficients are not probabilities. But their size and direction still matter: they determine where each country sits on the S-shaped normal CDF – the \(\Phi\) curve – and how far a one-unit change in a predictor slides it along that curve. The magnitude sets how steeply the probability responds; the sign sets whether it rises or falls. We saw in Figure 5 that the marginal effect (the change in the predicted probability of the outcome, \(y\), for a one-unit change in the independent variable, \(x\)) is not constant across the values of \(x\). In the present context, this means that a change in the probability to be democratic is different for every country, because each sits at a different point on the \(\Phi\) curve: the same nudge in GDP moves the probability a great deal in the steep middle of the curve and barely at all out in its flat tails. There is no single observation-invariant marginal effect: the marginal effect varies across observations. We can nevertheless summarize those effects, for example by taking their sample average.
This is exactly what the marginaleffects package (Arel-Bundock et al., 2024) is built for. For a fitted model it calculates those observation-by-observation effects, attaches standard errors to them via the delta method, and then summarises them. The most common summary is the average marginal effect (AME): the mean of the individual marginal effects across the sample. (One could instead evaluate the effect at specified representative covariate values – for example, with continuous predictors set to their means – but averaging the per-country effects is the more defensible default, since it uses the data as they actually are.)

library(marginaleffects)

# AME of logged GDP per capita on Pr(Democracy), within each resource group
avg_slopes(probit6, variables = "log.gdppc", by = "resource_state")


 resource_state Estimate Std. Error     z Pr(>|z|)    S   2.5 % 97.5 %
 Low Resources    0.0990     0.0295 3.354   <0.001 10.3  0.0411  0.157
 High Resources   0.0371     0.0392 0.945    0.345  1.5 -0.0398  0.114

Term: log.gdppc
Type: response
Comparison: dY/dX

# The average marginal *interaction* effect (cf. Ai & Norton 2003)
avg_slopes(probit6, variables = "log.gdppc", by = "resource_state",
           hypothesis = ~pairwise)


                         Hypothesis Estimate Std. Error     z Pr(>|z|)   S
 (High Resources) - (Low Resources)  -0.0619     0.0491 -1.26    0.207 2.3
  2.5 % 97.5 %
 -0.158 0.0343

Type: response


The function avg_slopes() is the AME workhorse. Its first argument is the fitted model; variables = "log.gdppc" tells it which predictor to differentiate the predicted probability with respect to; and by = "resource_state" asks it to average those per-country slopes separately within low- and high-resource states rather than pooling them. The first call therefore returns two AMEs, one per resource group. The second call adds hypothesis = ~pairwise, which compares the two group-specific AMEs and tests whether they differ. That difference is a sample-average summary of how GDP’s probability-scale effect varies across the observed resource groups. It is therefore the quantity we need when asking whether GDP behaves differently across resource environments, although it is not simply \(\beta_3\) translated onto the probability scale.
Reading the first table, each row is one resource group, and the numbers are the AMEs of logged GDP per capita on the probability of being a democracy.

Estimate is the AME itself: in low-resource states a one-unit rise in logged GDP raises the probability of democracy by about 0.099 on average, against only 0.037 in high-resource states (and recall that one unit of logged GDP is a large move — roughly a 2.7-fold change in GDP per capita).
Std. Error, z and Pr(>|z|) are the delta-method standard error, test statistic, and p-value for each average marginal effect. You can interpret them just as you would in a regression table: they tell us how much uncertainty surrounds the estimated effect, and whether it differs convincingly from zero. Here, the low-resource effect is clearly significant (z = 3.35, p < 0.001), while the high-resource effect is not (z = 0.94, p = 0.345).
Following Greenland’s S-value interpretation, the s-value, \(S=-\log_2(p)\), can be read as the number of consecutive heads in fair-coin tosses that would have the same probability as the observed \(p\)-value. It therefore puts the \(p\)-value on a more concrete scale (see Greenland, 2019, p. 109). Take a coin you are assuming is fair: a run of \(n\) heads in a row has probability \((1/2)^n\), so the longer the unbroken run, the harder it becomes to keep believing the coin is fair. The s-value is the run length whose probability equals your p-value — “the coin is fair” stands in for your null hypothesis, and “how many heads in a row” measures how hard the data push against it.

\(S\) tells us nothing the p-value doesn’t – it is the same number relabelled – but this scale is harder to misread than a bare probability, and it discourages treating \(p = 0.05\) as a sacrosanct threshold, since that cut-off is only about four heads in a row. To see why, solve \((1/2)^n=0.05\) for \(n\): \[\begin{align*}
0.5^n &= 0.05 \\[0.5ex]
\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n &= \frac{1}{20} \\[0.5ex]
\frac{1}{2^n} &= \frac{1}{20} \\[0.5ex]
2^n &= 20 \\[0.5ex]
n &= \log_2 20 \\[0.5ex]
n &\approx 4.32
\end{align*}\]

Low Resources scores \(S = 10.3\), a run that long being genuinely hard to square with a fair coin and so hard to put down to chance, whereas High Resources scores just \(S = 1.5\), scarcely more than a single toss and hence unremarkable.
The final 2.5 % and 97.5 % columns give the 95% confidence interval; note the high-resource interval runs from -0.040 to 0.114, comfortably spanning zero, while the low-resource one (0.041 to 0.157) lies entirely above zero. The footer lines Term: log.gdppc, Type: response and Comparison: dY/dX confirm that what’s reported is the slope (dY/dX) of log.gdppc, expressed in actual probabilities (response) rather than as movement along the \(\Phi\) curve. In the second table the single row, labelled (High Resources) − (Low Resources), is the difference between the two AMEs — here 0.037 − 0.099 ≈ -0.062 — with its own test (p = 0.207); that is the line that tells us whether the interaction is significant in actual probabilities, and here it is not.

In substance this is a resource-curse pattern: income predicts democracy where resource rents are low but does essentially nothing where they are high. The test that settles whether that contrast is real is the average marginal interaction effect in the second table, and it cannot reject the null — so in actual probabilities we cannot say the GDP effect genuinely differs across resource environments. This is the \(\beta_3\) caveat made concrete: the coefficient is significant at the 5% level (\(\beta_3 = -0.366\), \(p < 0.05\)), yet the interaction in actual probabilities is not. Had we read the interaction straight off \(\beta_3\) — as we legitimately could in the linear model — we would have drawn the wrong substantive conclusion.

Categorical \(\times\) Categorical, and Continuous \(\times\) Continuous

Everything we just did carries over to the other variable-type combinations, with the same twist each time: \(\beta_3\) describes movement along the \(\Phi\) curve, not a change in probability, so the substantive interaction has to be recovered with marginal effects, never read straight off \(\beta_3\).

I have summarised the different interaction types for probit in Table 8 (so it is the probit counterpart of Table 4). I will then take you through the remaining cases – Categorical \(\times\) Categorical, and Continuous \(\times\) Continuous – in a numerical example below.



Table 8: Interaction Types (Probit)










Scenario
Interpretation of \(\beta_3\) (movement along the \(\Phi\) curve)
A useful probability-scale interaction summary




Continuous \(\times\) Categorical
How differently does a one-unit change in the continuous variable slide a country along the \(\Phi\) curve from one category to the other?  e.g. Does a rise in GDP slide a country towards democracy more steeply in high- than in low-resource states?
Difference in the average marginal effect of the continuous variable across categories


Categorical \(\times\) Categorical
How far does belonging to both categories shift a country along the \(\Phi\) curve, over and above the two single-category shifts?  e.g. Does the resource effect on democracy differ between high- and low-income states?
Difference-in-differences of predicted probabilities across the four cells — not \(\beta_3\)


Continuous \(\times\) Continuous
How much does the distance one continuous variable slides a country along the \(\Phi\) curve change per unit of the other?  e.g. Does the GDP effect on democracy change with resource dependence?
Difference in the average marginal effect evaluated at selected moderator values (e.g. mean, \(\pm 1\) SD)






 
For an interaction between two categorical variables, we need a second dummy. To stay with the previous example, let’s split GDP per capita at its median and ask whether the effect of resource dependence on the probability of democracy depends on a country’s income level:

world <- world %>%
  mutate(income_state = factor(
    ifelse(gdppc > median(gdppc, na.rm = TRUE), "High Income", "Low Income"),
    levels = c("Low Income", "High Income")))

probit7 <- glm(democracy ~ income_state * resource_state,
               data = world, family = binomial(link = "probit"))

Formally,
\[\begin{equation*}
\Pr(\text{Democracy}_i = 1) = \Phi\!\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{HighIncome}_i + \beta_2 \text{HighResources}_i + \beta_3\,(\text{HighIncome}_i \cdot \text{HighResources}_i)\right)
\end{equation*}\]

It pays to familiarise yourself with this way of notation, as we will come back to this in Week 7, when we make our probit model fit for modelling time.

In the linear cat \(\times\) cat model we could read the interaction straight off \(\beta_3\) and picture the four group means as a bar chart. In a probit neither shortcut works: the four cells now hold predicted probabilities rather than means, and \(\beta_3\) lives on the index scale. So we work with the four predicted probabilities directly — but the underlying logic of an interaction is exactly the same.
With two binary variables we have a 2×2 grid: low or high income, crossed with low or high resources, giving a predicted probability of democracy in each of the four cells. The effect of resources is a difference — the probability of democracy in high-resource states minus the probability in low-resource states. The trick is that we can calculate that difference twice: once among low-income countries and once among high-income countries. If resources matter by the same amount regardless of income, those two differences will be equal; if they are not equal, the effect of resources depends on income — and “the effect of one thing depends on another” is precisely what an interaction is.
The single number that captures this is the difference between those two differences — the difference-in-differences3. It is simply the categorical interaction expressed on the probability scale: a value of zero means no interaction (resources do the same work in rich and poor countries alike), and the further it sits from zero, the more the resource effect hinges on income. So rather than reading \(\beta_3\), we calculate the four predicted probabilities and then test their difference-in-differences:

# Predicted probability of democracy in each of the four cells

predictions(probit7, by = c("income_state", "resource_state"))

Moving from low to high resource dependence changes the probability of being a democracy by -0.313 among low-income states (0.379 − 0.692) and by -0.432 among high-income states (0.462 − 0.894). Whether these two effects differ — the difference-in-differences, which is the categorical interaction expressed in probabilities — is -0.119 (\(p = 0.43\)). As it is insignificant in this case, we conclude that the effect of resource dependence on the probability of democracy does not depend on a country’s income level.

As before, this is the quantity to report, not the coefficient \(\beta_3\) = -0.533 (\(p = 0.23\)) on its own.

For an interaction between two continuous variables, we can surprisingly mirror the logic of the linear case exactly: there is an infinite family of slopes, so we evaluate the marginal effect of one variable at low (−1 SD), average, and high (+1 SD) values of the other — only now on the probability scale. The model is:
\[\begin{equation*}
\Pr(\text{Democracy}_i = 1) = \Phi\!\left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 \log\text{GDPpc}_i + \beta_2 \log\text{Rents}_i + \beta_3\,(\log\text{GDPpc}_i \cdot \log\text{Rents}_i)\right)
\end{equation*}\]

probit8 <- glm(democracy ~ log.gdppc * log.natural,
               data = world, family = binomial(link = "probit"))

In the linear case, sim_slopes() did the work for us: it chose low, typical, and high values of the moderator – one standard deviation below the mean, the mean, and one above – and reported the slope of GDP at each. We want those same three numbers here, but a probit has no interactions-style shortcut, so we have to assemble them from two marginaleffects functions.
We first take the mean and standard deviation of the moderator – here log(resource rents) – over the observations actually used in the model, which allows us to calculate low / typical / high values to plug in. datagrid() then builds a small set of hypothetical countries, one for each of those three values, holding everything else at a typical level – here, log(per capita GDP) at its mean (Arel-Bundock et al., 2024). slopes() finally calculates the marginal effect of log(per capita GDP) – the change in the predicted probability of democracy for a one-unit increase – at each of those three scenarios. The result is the effect of GDP at low, average, and high resource dependence: exactly what sim_slopes() gave us, only now as a change in probability rather than a single straight-line slope.
One thing here differs from the linear case, however. In the linear model a single slope described the effect of GDP for every country: a one-unit increase shifted the outcome by the same amount no matter where a country started. In a probit that is no longer true. Recall that the same step in GDP moves the probability a great deal in the steep middle of the \(\Phi\) curve and barely at all out in its flat tails — and a country’s own level of GDP is part of what decides where on that curve it sits. So the effect of GDP is genuinely larger for some countries than for others. This is why, even after we have fixed the level of resource rents, there is still no single “effect of GDP” to quote: we also have to pin GDP somewhere. The natural choice is a country of average income — so each figure below is the effect of GDP for a typical-income country at the stated level of resource dependence. s <- sd(model.frame(probit8)$log.natural)

You take the effect of resources among low-income states (one difference of predicted probabilities), the effect of resources among high-income states (a second difference), and subtract them. The result tells you whether the resource effect depends on income — i.e. it’s the categorical \(\times\) categorical interaction, expressed in probabilities. No causal claim, no time dimension, no intervention. A DiD design (Card–Krueger minimum wage, that whole tradition) uses the same arithmetic but adds a great deal on top. So yes, you just need to strip away the treatment-and-time structure and the parallel-trends assumption, and you’re left with just the subtraction-of-two-subtractions, which is what we are doing here.↩︎

title: Part I: Country Fixed Effects Models with Driscoll-Kraay Standard Errors
text:
Why not just Ordinary Least Squares?
You learned about linear regression, and the method of Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) in Week 2. I mentioned back then, that there are a number of assumptions you are agreeing to whenever you estimate such a model, and two of those are becoming especially problematic when we start introducing time into our data.
crumbs: 9  Part I: Country Fixed Effects Models with Driscoll-Kraay Standard Errors

title: Part I: Country Fixed Effects Models with Driscoll-Kraay Standard Errors
text:
Serial Autocorrelation
A country’s Polity V score in 2010 is not independent of its score in 2009, or 2005. Institutional change is gradual. Whatever unmeasured factors drove Nigeria’s score last year are likely still present this year. If we treat repeated observations on the same country as if they were independent data points from entirely separate entities, we are ignoring the strong possibility of autocorrelation (of error terms).
Autocorrelation means that the error terms are correlated with each other over time. Think about what the error term represents: everything that affects democracy but is not captured by your independent variables. For any given country, these omitted factors — political culture, the strength of civil society, the legacy of colonial institutions — tend to be persistent. They do not suddenly vanish from one year to the next. This means that if the model underestimates a country’s democracy score in year \(t\), it is likely to underestimate it in year \(t+1\) as well, because the same unmeasured forces are still at work.
If you want this more technically – we will get to this in more detail further below – OLS assumes no serial correlation in the error term within units: \(\text{Cov}(\epsilon_{it}, \epsilon_{is}) = 0\) for \(t \neq s\). In panel data this assumption is routinely violated. Plain OLS standard errors will generally be unreliable, often too small in positively correlated panel settings, which can inflate test statistics, make your p-values too low, and lead you to reject null hypotheses you should not reject.
crumbs: 9  Part I: Country Fixed Effects Models with Driscoll-Kraay Standard Errors

title: Part I: Country Fixed Effects Models with Driscoll-Kraay Standard Errors
text:
Cross-Sectional Dependence
Countries are not hermetically sealed. They share regions, colonial histories, alliance structures, and exposure to global shocks. The post-Cold War democratic wave of 1989–1993 hit Eastern Europe simultaneously. The Arab Spring in 2011 simultaneously affected Tunisia, Egypt, Libya, and others. In a cross-sectional model these shared shocks end up in the error term. If many countries have correlated errors at the same point in time, our standard errors are again wrong.
Once again, more technically, OLS assumes \(\text{Cov}(\epsilon_{it}, \epsilon_{jt}) = 0\) for \(i \neq j\) (for all \(t\)). In country-year panel data this assumption is also routinely violated, with the same consequence: standard errors that are too small.
crumbs: 9  Part I: Country Fixed Effects Models with Driscoll-Kraay Standard Errors

title: Part I: Country Fixed Effects Models with Driscoll-Kraay Standard Errors
text:
Step 1: Declaring the Panel Structure
The first thing we must do is tell R that our data has a panel structure. We do this with pdata.frame(), which creates a special kind of data frame that R understands as indexed by a unit and a time variable.

pdata <- pdata.frame(your_data, index = c("country", "year"))

The index argument takes a vector of two variable names. The first is always the unit identifier, the second is always the time identifier. Once this is done, plm functions can exploit the panel structure automatically.

This step is easy to overlook, but it is not optional. If you pass a plain data frame to the model function plm() in the next step, R will either produce an error or silently produce wrong results. Always declare the panel structure first.
crumbs: 9  Part I: Country Fixed Effects Models with Driscoll-Kraay Standard Errors

title: Part I: Country Fixed Effects Models with Driscoll-Kraay Standard Errors
text:
Step 2: Estimating the Model
The plm() function works very similarly to lm(). The syntax for the formula is identical — dependent variable on the left of the tilde, independent variables on the right, separated by +. The key difference is the model argument:

model <- plm(polity5 ~ gdppc + enrol_gross + oil,
             data  = pdata,
             model = "pooling")

model = "pooling" tells R to estimate a pooled OLS model – it stacks all country-year observations and estimates a single OLS regression, exactly as lm() would do, but now using the declared panel structure.

Pooling
The combining of observations across multiple units and time periods into a single dataset. A pooled OLS estimator treats all observations as independent and does not account for unobserved heterogeneity across units, which can lead to biased and inconsistent estimates if such heterogeneity is present. Furthermore, observations within the same unit are likely correlated across time, violating the assumption of independent errors and necessitating the use of cluster-robust standard errors.

We use plm rather than lm here because plm is what allows us to apply the Driscoll-Kraay correction in the next step.
crumbs: 9  Part I: Country Fixed Effects Models with Driscoll-Kraay Standard Errors

title: Part I: Country Fixed Effects Models with Driscoll-Kraay Standard Errors
section: Step 3: Calculate the Driscoll-Kraay Standard Errors
text:
Step 3: Calculate the Driscoll-Kraay Standard Errors
The root for this correction lives in a separate object – a so-called variance-covariance matrix – calculated by vcovSCC() from the plm package (Millo, 2017). Before we look at the code, it is worth understanding what a variance-covariance matrix actually is, because the term appears repeatedly in the output of statistical software and in methods papers, yet is rarely explained in plain language.

What is a Variance-Covariance Matrix?
You already know what a variance is: it is a measure of how spread out a variable is around its mean. In the context of regression, the variance of a coefficient \(\hat{\beta}\) tells you how much that estimate would vary if you drew many different samples from the same population and re-ran the regression each time. A small variance means the estimate is stable and precise; a large variance means it is sensitive to which particular observations happened to end up in your sample. The square root of this variance is, of course, the standard error – the quantity that appears in your regression output and determines the width of your confidence intervals.
Now, in a multiple regression model you have several coefficients – say \(\hat{\beta}_1\) for GDP per capita, \(\hat{\beta}_2\) for education, and \(\hat{\beta}_3\) for oil rents. Each of these has its own variance. But there is something else: the estimates can be correlated with each other.

Correlation
A standardised measure of the linear relationship between two variables (\(x_i\) and \(y_i\)), bounded between \(-1\) and \(1\), which indicates both the direction and strength of their association.

If GDP per capita and education are highly correlated in your data, then the estimate of \(\hat{\beta}_1\) and the estimate of \(\hat{\beta}_2\) will tend to move together across different samples — when one is overestimated, the other tends to be overestimated too. This shared movement is captured by the covariance between the two coefficients.

Covariance
A measure which assesses the degree to which the values of two variables (\(x_i\) and \(y_i\)) vary together (their joint variability).

A Variance-Covariance Matrix (sometimes shortened to “VCV matrix” or just “vcov”) collects all of this information in a single object. It is a square matrix — one row and one column for each coefficient in your model. The diagonal entries are the variances of each individual coefficient. The off-diagonal entries are the covariances between pairs of coefficients. Here is what it looks like schematically for a model with three coefficients:
\[
\text{Var-Cov} =
\begin{bmatrix}
\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_1) & \text{Cov}(\hat{\beta}_1, \hat{\beta}_2) & \text{Cov}(\hat{\beta}_1, \hat{\beta}_3) \\
\text{Cov}(\hat{\beta}_2, \hat{\beta}_1) & \text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_2) & \text{Cov}(\hat{\beta}_2, \hat{\beta}_3) \\
\text{Cov}(\hat{\beta}_3, \hat{\beta}_1) & \text{Cov}(\hat{\beta}_3, \hat{\beta}_2) & \text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_3)
\end{bmatrix}
\]
You will notice the matrix is symmetric — the covariance of \(\hat{\beta}_1\) with \(\hat{\beta}_2\) is the same as the covariance of \(\hat{\beta}_2\) with \(\hat{\beta}_1\), so the upper-right triangle mirrors the lower-left triangle.
For our purposes, the most important thing to understand is that the standard errors you see in regression output are simply the square roots of the diagonal entries of the variance-covariance matrix. When we say that Driscoll-Kraay produces corrected standard errors, what we mean technically is that it produces a different variance-covariance matrix – one whose diagonal entries more accurately reflect the true uncertainty in the coefficient estimates, given the autocorrelation and cross-sectional dependence in the data. Everything else – the coefficients themselves, the t-statistics, the p-values – then flows from this corrected matrix.
This is why the correction lives in a separate object in R, rather than being built into the model itself. The model (plm()) produces the coefficient estimates. The variance-covariance matrix (vcovSCC()) provides the uncertainty estimates. And coeftest() brings them together to produce the final output you report.

Variance-Covariance Matrix
It is a table that tells you the precision of each coefficient estimate (the diagonal) and the degree to which the estimates are correlated with each other (the off-diagonal). The standard errors in your output are the square roots of the diagonal entries.

With this knowledge in mind, the code for calculating the Driscoll-Kraay version of this matrix is straightforward: “SCC” stands for Spatial and Serial Correlation Consistent (see Millo, 2017, pp. 8–9), which is exactly what Driscoll-Kraay provides.

dk_vcov <- vcovSCC(model, type = "HC3", cluster = "time")

The arguments here are as follows:

type = "HC3" tells the function exactly how to calculate the penalty mathematically. HC3 is the default option in the sandwich package which you might recognise from dealing with heteroscedasticity on PO12Q which is why I am selecting it here.
cluster = "time" tells vcovSCC to cluster by the time dimension, which is the correct choice for Driscoll-Kraay.
crumbs: 9  Part I: Country Fixed Effects Models with Driscoll-Kraay Standard Errors

title: Part I: Country Fixed Effects Models with Driscoll-Kraay Standard Errors
section: Step 4: Applying the Corrected Standard Errors
text:
Step 4: Applying the Corrected Standard Errors
This is where students most commonly make a mistake. If you call summary(model) without any additional arguments, R will display the uncorrected OLS standard errors – as if you had never calculated dk_vcov. The correction must be passed explicitly every time you inspect or report results:

coeftest(model, vcov = dk_vcov)

coeftest() from the lmtest package re-calculates the t-statistics and p-values using the corrected variance-covariance matrix. This is the output you should read and report.

A common Mistake
summary(model) will always show plain OLS standard errors, regardless of whether you have calculated a Driscoll-Kraay correction. Always use coeftest(model, vcov = dk_vcov) to inspect results, and always pass vcov = dk_vcov when producing regression tables. Forgetting this step means you are reporting numbers that do not reflect the correction you intended to make.

title: Part I: Country Fixed Effects Models with Driscoll-Kraay Standard Errors
text:
Interpreting the Output
The output of coeftest() will look familiar. It has the same structure as the output you have already seen from lm(): a row for the intercept and a row for each independent variable, with columns for the estimate, the standard error, the t-statistic, and the p-value.
The interpretation of the coefficients is identical to what you learned in the cross-sectional context:

Is the coefficient significant? Check the p-value in the Pr(>|t|) column. If it is below 0.05, you have evidence to reject the null hypothesis. If it is above 0.05, you cannot claim a statistically significant relationship. The coefficient for log_gdppc is highly statistically significant, so we can proceed to the next step.
If significant, what is the direction? A positive coefficient means that higher values of the independent variable are associated with higher Polity V scores; a negative coefficient means the reverse.
What is the size of the effect? Because we have logged GDP per capita, the coefficient is interpreted as follows: a one unit increase in log GDP per capita is associated with a change of \(\hat{\beta}\) units in the Polity V score, on average, holding all other variables constant.

section: A Note on plm and the tidyverse
text:
A Note on plm and the tidyverse
You may have noticed that the code above performs all the lag construction on the plain data frame df, before declaring the panel structure with pdata.frame(). This is deliberate, and it is worth understanding why.
The pdata.frame object is a special class that stores the panel index as both attributes and hidden columns. When you pipe a pdata.frame through dplyr verbs – such as group_by(), mutate(), arrange(), or filter() – dplyr does not know how to preserve this structure. It quietly converts your data back into an ordinary data frame, throwing away the special pdata.frame structure that plm() relies on. In doing so it can drop or scramble the index columns – the ones that tell R which rows belong to which country and year – and even reorder the rows themselves. Once that panel structure is gone, plm() no longer knows how your data are organised, so when you feed the object back in you will usually get a warning like:
Warning in pdata.frame(data, index = index, ...) :
  duplicate couples (id-time) in resulting pdata.frame
There is also a more subtle issue. Both dplyr and plm feature a function called lag(), and they behave very differently. dplyr::lag() is a positional shift: it moves values up by one row, with no awareness of panel structure. plm’s lag() is panel-aware: it respects the country grouping and the time ordering automatically. Whichever package you loaded last wins the namespace, and because library(tidyverse) is typically loaded after library(plm), dplyr::lag() usually masks plm::lag(). R will tell you this on startup, but it is easy to miss. This is why the code above calls dplyr::lag() explicitly: it removes any ambiguity about which function is being used.
The safest workflow, and the one we adopt throughout this module, is therefore the following:

Load your data into a plain data frame.
Perform all, and I mean ALL, data preparation – variable transformations, lag construction, filtering, joining – using tidyverse functions on this plain data frame.
Declare the panel structure with pdata.frame() as the final step of data preparation before you start estimating models.
Pass the pdata.frame directly to plm() and do not modify it further.


If you find yourself wanting to manipulate a pdata.frame with dplyr verbs, then it is imperative that you resist that temptation! Instead, go back to the plain data frame, do the work there, and run your RScript from that point to where you initially left off.

title: Part II: Markov Transition Models with Correlated Random Effects
text:
Introduction
If – like me – you think that there is a minimum requirement, a threshold at which democracy ceases to exist, then you are in the world in which democracy is a binary concept. In this case, linear regression is unsuitable, because a binary dependent variable violates key assumptions of OLS and can generate predicted probabilities outside the feasible 0–1 range. This consideration led us to probit models in Week 3. But a standard probit model does not naturally distinguish between the processes of democratic emergence and democratic survival. When our question concerns transitions between regime states over time, we need a model that explicitly conditions on the previous regime type. This is where Markov Transition Models come in.
crumbs: 10  Part II: Markov Transition Models with Correlated Random Effects

title: Part II: Markov Transition Models with Correlated Random Effects
text:
Conditional Probabilities
Conditional probability express what I have described before in a formal way. The conditional probability to model for democratic emergence is written as follows:
\[\begin{equation}
P(y_{i,t} = 1 | y_{i, t-1} = 0)
\end{equation}\]
This reads: The probability of a country i to be a democracy (y=1) in year t, given (this is what the vertical line | says) that country i was an autocracy (y=0) in the previous year (t-1). Analogously, the conditional probability for democratic survival is:
\[\begin{equation}
P(y_{i,t} = 1 | y_{i, t-1} = 1)
\end{equation}\]
This reads: The probability of a country i to be a democracy (y=1) in year t, given that country i was also a democracy (y=1) in the previous year (t-1).

Conditional Probability
The probability of an event occurring given that another event has already occurred, written \(P(A|B)\), where the vertical bar is read as “given”. In a Markov Transition Model, the conditional probability \(P(y_{i,t} = 1 | y_{i,t-1} = 0)\) expresses the probability of a country being a democracy in year \(t\), given that it was an autocracy in year \(t-1\).

We will now apply this knowledge to create a model in R which calculates these conditional probabilities. Let’s start with democratic emergence.
crumbs: 10  Part II: Markov Transition Models with Correlated Random Effects

title: Part II: Markov Transition Models with Correlated Random Effects
text:
Democratic Emergence
Democratic emergence is expressed as the probability of a country to be a democracy in year \(t\), given that it was a dictatorship in the previous year, \(t-1\)
\[\begin{equation*}
P(y_{i,t} = 1 | y_{i, t-1} = 0)
\end{equation*}\]
As a first step, we therefore need a variable that gives us the information which regime type each of our countries had in the previous year. We will use the world data set for this illustration.

world <- read.csv("world.csv")

library(tidyverse)

We can now create the lagged democracy value. In order for R to know when a new country “starts”, we need to group observations by country first, and then lag the variable democracy. We do this with the intuitively called function lag(). We then ungroup the data again, as we have no need of the groups any more.

world <- world %>%
  group_by(countrycode) %>%
  mutate(l.democracy = lag(democracy)) %>%
  ungroup()

This creates a new variable l.democracy which gives us the information we were after: the regime type of the country in the previous year. Note that as the first observation for each country cannot be lagged, it creates as many missing values as we have countries in the data set. Perhaps this makes more sense with a visualisation:
 



Schematic of lagged variable

title: Part II: Markov Transition Models with Correlated Random Effects
text:
Lagging the Independent Variables
So far, we have lagged the dependent variable, to run an MTM. This was a methodological necessity. But from a substantive point of view it makes sense to also lag our independent variables. It is reasonable to assume, that the regime type in year \(t\) depends on the state of socio-economic development in the previous year, \(t-1\). It is rare that for example a recession hits, and the country immediately changes regime type. These things need time. And this is why we will now also lag the independent variables. Before I do this, let me create the logarithmised version of per capita GDP, however (see Week 4):

world$log_gdppc <- log(world$gdppc)

Since the code for lagging each independent variable follows the same pattern, we can create the lags for all three in one go.
At the same time, we are going to calculate the over-time average for each of these variables for every country. As we will see later, including these country-specific averages allows us to implement a Correlated Random Effects (CRE) model, which prevents our estimates from being distorted by deep-seated, unobserved country differences (like political culture or geography).
Crucially, we must calculate these averages now, across the entire dataset, before we split our data into separate transition states.

world <- world %>%
  group_by(countrycode) %>%
  mutate(
    # 1. Substantive Lags
    l.log_gdppc    = lag(log_gdppc),
    l.life         = lag(life),
    l.enrol_gross  = lag(enrol_gross),
    l.gdppc_growth = lag(gdppc_growth),
    
    # 2. Country-Specific Averages (CRE Mundlak terms)
    mean_log_gdppc    = mean(log_gdppc, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_life         = mean(life, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_enrol_gross  = mean(enrol_gross, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_gdppc_growth = mean(gdppc_growth, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()


Remember when writing the assessment in general, and the methods section in particular, that lagging the independent variables is not a methodological consideration, but a substantive one. It has nothing to do with the Markov Transition Model itself.

Interpretation

title: Part II: Markov Transition Models with Correlated Random Effects
text:
Why Standard Errors Need Adjusting
When we estimate our emergence and survival models, R calculates standard errors for each coefficient. These standard errors are used to determine whether a coefficient is statistically significant. By default, glm() assumes that all errors in our data are independent of one another. In our case, this assumption is almost certainly wrong.
Think about what our data look like. We have many observations per country, one for each year. Is it reasonable to assume that what happens in Brazil in 1995 is completely unrelated to what happens in Brazil in 1994? Of course not. A country’s political situation in one year is heavily shaped by what came before, and any unmeasured factors driving Brazil’s situation in 1994 are very likely still at work in 1995. This produces what is called serial correlation, or autocorrelation (of error terms): the errors from the same country end up correlated with one another over time, rather than being independent as glm() assumes.

Correlation
A standardised measure of the linear relationship between two variables (\(x_i\) and \(y_i\)), bounded between \(-1\) and \(1\), which indicates both the direction and strength of their association.
 
Autocorrelation
Autocorrelation occurs when the values of error terms are correlated across observations.

When the errors within a country are correlated, the default standard errors produced by glm() tend to be too small. This means we would conclude that a coefficient is statistically significant when in fact we cannot be confident that it is. In other words, we would be too quick to reject the null hypothesis.

Why CRE Cannot Solve This
A Markov Transition model makes today’s regime type dependent on the regime type in the previous period. But countries also differ in many stable, unobserved ways—such as their historical legacies or deep institutional setups. If we ignore these factors, they slip into the error term and create two distinct problems: coefficient bias and incorrect standard errors.
CRE can only address the coefficient bias. It adds the country-specific averages of our variables (mean_log_gdppc, etc.) directly into our model, which absorb the stable, long-term differences between countries. This leaves our lagged variables (l.log_gdppc) free to measure pure within-country changes over time, completely purging our main coefficients of unobserved country bias.
But unbiased coefficients are only half of what we need. The default standard errors reported by glm() assume that every observation is independent — yet observations from the same country remain correlated over time even after the country means are included (autocorrelation in the errors). CRE does nothing about this: it corrects the value of the coefficient, but does not determine how its uncertainty is calculated. This leaves its reported precision overstated, and we need to find a different way to address this issue.
crumbs: 10  Part II: Markov Transition Models with Correlated Random Effects

title: Part II: Markov Transition Models with Correlated Random Effects
text:
Clustering Standard Errors by Country
The solution is to use cluster-robust standard errors, where we define a country as a cluster. Rather than assuming all observations are independent, this approach allows observations within the same country to be correlated with one another, whilst still assuming independence across countries after conditioning on the covariates — an assumption that may be violated when global shocks affect many countries simultaneously. The standard errors are then adjusted accordingly, and tend to be larger and more conservative than the default.

Cluster-Robust Standard Errors
Standard errors that are adjusted to account for the fact that observations within the same group (or cluster) are correlated with one another, whilst assuming independence across groups. In panel data, countries typically serve as clusters, since repeated observations on the same country are unlikely to be independent over time. Cluster-robust standard errors are generally larger and more conservative than default standard errors, reflecting the reduced effective information content of correlated observations.

In R, we can calculate cluster-robust standard errors using the vcovCL() function from the sandwich package. We do not re-estimate the models themselves — the coefficients remain exactly the same. What changes is how we calculate the uncertainty around those coefficients. To understand what vcovCL() is actually doing – and why the correction lives in a separate object in R, rather than being built into the model itself – it helps to know what a Variance-Covariance Matrix is.
You already know what a variance is: a measure of how spread out a variable is around its mean. In the context of probit, the variance of a coefficient \(\hat{\beta}\) tells you how much that estimate would vary if you drew many different samples from the same population and re-ran the model each time. A small variance means the estimate is stable and precise; a large variance means it is sensitive to which particular observations happened to end up in your sample. The square root of this variance is the standard error – the quantity that appears in your output and determines the width of your confidence intervals.
But in a model with several coefficients, there is something else as well: the estimates can be correlated with each other. If two variables in the model are themselves highly correlated — as l.urban and l.agri plausibly are — then the estimates \(\hat{\beta}_1\) and \(\hat{\beta}_2\) will tend to move together across repeated samples: when one is overestimated, the other tends to be overestimated too. This shared movement is captured by the covariance between the two coefficients.

Covariance
A measure which assesses the degree to which the values of two variables (\(x_i\) and \(y_i\)) vary together (their joint variability).

A Variance-Covariance Matrix collects all of this information in a single object. It is a square matrix – one row and one column for each coefficient in your model. The diagonal entries are the variances of each individual coefficient. The off-diagonal entries are the covariances between pairs of coefficients. Schematically, for a model with three coefficients it looks like this:
\[
\text{Var-Cov} =
\begin{bmatrix}
\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_1) & \text{Cov}(\hat{\beta}_1, \hat{\beta}_2) & \text{Cov}(\hat{\beta}_1, \hat{\beta}_3) \\
\text{Cov}(\hat{\beta}_2, \hat{\beta}_1) & \text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_2) & \text{Cov}(\hat{\beta}_2, \hat{\beta}_3) \\
\text{Cov}(\hat{\beta}_3, \hat{\beta}_1) & \text{Cov}(\hat{\beta}_3, \hat{\beta}_2) & \text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_3)
\end{bmatrix}
\]
The matrix is symmetric – the covariance of \(\hat{\beta}_1\) with \(\hat{\beta}_2\) is the same as the covariance of \(\hat{\beta}_2\) with \(\hat{\beta}_1\). The standard errors you see in regression output are simply the square roots of the diagonal entries. The off-diagonal entries usually fade into the background, but bear them in mind, as we will need them later on when we are constructing a results table that contains the correct standard errors of the survival slopes.

Variance-Covariance Matrix
A table that tells you the precision of each coefficient estimate (the diagonal) and the degree to which the estimates are correlated with each other (the off-diagonal). The standard errors in your output are the square roots of the diagonal entries.

The default standard errors in your glm() output are the square roots of the diagonal entries of a default variance-covariance matrix – one that assumes independence across all observations. What the aforementioned vcovCL() function does is calculate a different variance-covariance matrix, one whose diagonal entries more accurately reflect the true uncertainty in the coefficient estimates given the within-country correlation in the data. The coefficient estimates themselves don’t change. Everything else – the standard errors, the z-statistics, the p-values, and any joint tests – then flows from this corrected matrix.
To display the results from the glm() output with the uncertainty estimates of the the variance-covariance matrix (vcovCL()) in the form you are used to from calling the summary() function, we can use the coeftest() function:

Two things are worth noting here. First, notice the cluster = ~ countrycode argument. Think of this as a safety mechanism for your data. When you run a model, R automatically drops any row containing a missing value, meaning the dataset you started with is often different from the dataset the model actually used.
If you were to pass the cluster as a simple vector (world_democ1$countrycode), you would be handing R a list that is too long, causing the clusters to misalign with the rows the model actually estimated. By passing the cluster as a one-sided formula (~ countrycode), you are telling R to look inside the model object itself to find the data. This guarantees that your cluster labels and your observations are perfectly synchronized—the formula interface automatically “cleans” the cluster list to match the model’s survivors, preventing the silent errors that happen when rows are dropped.
Second, the type = "HC3" argument applies a more conservative small-sample correction than the commonly used HC1. Unless you do a global analysis in your assessment, the the regional data sets only cover a relatively small number of countries, which makes HC3 the more appropriate choice: it downweights influential clusters and guards against underestimating uncertainty when the number of clusters is limited.

section: Passing the Adjusted Standard Errors to modelsummary
text:
Passing the Adjusted Standard Errors to modelsummary
When we use modelsummary to create results tables, we need to tell it to use our cluster-robust standard errors when calculating t-statistics, p-values, and significance stars, rather than the default ones stored in the model objects. To do this, you need to store the results of the vcovCL() calculations in a list:

vcov_list <- list(
  vcovCL(emergence, cluster = ~ countrycode, type = "HC3"),
  vcovCL(emergence_full, cluster = ~ countrycode, type = "HC3"),
  vcovCL(survival,  cluster = ~ countrycode, type = "HC3"),
  vcovCL(survival_full,  cluster = ~ countrycode, type = "HC3")
)

Then you feed this list into the modelsummary code:

modelsummary(..., 
             vcov = vcov_list, 
             ...)

Everything else in the modelsummary call remains the same. The coefficients you see in the table are identical to those from summary() – only the standard errors, and therefore the significance stars, may differ. I will provide you with an example when I explain how to put the full reults table together.

title: Part II: Markov Transition Models with Correlated Random Effects
text:
What about year fixed effects?
Clustering by country handles one type of dependence in the data: the fact that observations from the same country are correlated over time. It does not handle a second type: cross-country contemporaneous correlation, where all countries in a given year are affected by the same global shock — the end of the Cold War, the 2008 financial crisis, or a global democratisation wave. Year fixed effects (adding factor(year) to the model) are the standard solution to this problem, absorbing everything that happened in a given year and affected all countries simultaneously.

Year Fixed Effects
Indicator variables for each time period included in a regression model, which absorb everything that affected all units simultaneously in a given year. In cross-national panel data, year fixed effects account for global shocks that introduce contemporaneous correlation across countries. Their inclusion is a modelling choice rather than a default: if they are not jointly significant, they add little explanatory power, and in binary outcome models with sparse outcomes they can create estimation problems through complete separation.


Haven’t we already dealt with this by clustering?
No, because clustering and year fixed effects answer two different questions, even though both are about “dependence” in the data.
Think about the two ways observations can fail to be independent. The first runs down a country’s own column: Spain in 2001 looks a lot like Spain in 2000, because a country carries its history with it. That is within-country correlation over time, and it is what clustering by countrycode handles – it tells the standard errors not to treat Spain’s fifty-odd years as fifty independent facts.
The second runs across a row, through a single year: in 1989–91 a whole swathe of countries democratised together, and in a global recession many economies turn down at once. Here the observations are linked not because they share a country but because they share a moment – a common shock hitting everyone in the same year. Clustering by country does nothing about this, because the countries caught up in a given year’s wave sit in different clusters; the correlation runs between clusters, exactly where clustering assumes independence.
Year fixed effects – a dummy for each year, added with factor(year) – absorb whatever is common to all countries in that year, so each country’s result is measured relative to the global mood of its year rather than against an absolute baseline. That is why you may need both at once: clustering for the fact that a country resembles its own past, year effects for the fact that the world moves in unison.
But as I will show in a moment, needing them and being able to estimate them are not the same thing – but that is a separate problem from whether they are conceptually called for.

Before adding year fixed effects, it is worth checking whether they are jointly significant using a likelihood ratio test. We do this by estimating a model with and without year fixed effects and comparing them:

# Model without year fixed effects
emergence_no_fe <- glm(democracy ~ l.log_gdppc + l.gdppc_growth + 
                         mean_log_gdppc + mean_gdppc_growth,
                       data = world_democ0,
                       na.action = na.exclude,
                       family = binomial(link = "probit"))

# Model with year fixed effects
emergence_fe <- glm(democracy ~ l.log_gdppc + l.gdppc_growth + 
                         mean_log_gdppc + mean_gdppc_growth + factor(year),
                    data = world_democ0,
                    na.action = na.exclude,
                    family = binomial(link = "probit"))

# Likelihood ratio test
library(lmtest)
lrtest(emergence_no_fe, emergence_fe)

---

Since the p-value is below 0.05, the year fixed effects are jointly significant, suggesting that common year-specific shocks explain meaningful variation in the probability of democracy. In many applications, this would favour including them. However, in binary outcome models we must also check whether their inclusion creates estimation problems.

What does “jointly significant” mean substantively?
Each year dummy captures whatever affected all countries simultaneously in that year, such as the 2008 financial crisis mentioned above. Individually, most year dummies will look insignificant: a single year’s global turbulence rarely moves the needle on its own. But taken together, the year effects can absorb a meaningful share of the variation in democratic outcomes, and that is what the joint test detects.
A significant result is the data telling us that “what year it was” matters for the probability of democracy, over and above country-level factors. If the test had failed to reject, we could conclude that global shocks contributed little explanatory power in our sample and the year dummies could reasonably be omitted.

However, there is an important practical problem with year fixed effects in binary outcome models with sparse outcomes. In the emergence model, the sample (world_democ0) includes only country-years in which the country was autocratic in the previous year. We are therefore modelling the probability that a country becomes democratic conditional on having been autocratic at t − 1. Most observations in this sample remain autocratic, while only a comparatively small number transition to democracy. This creates a risk of complete separation when year fixed effects are added.

Why are year dummies especially vulnerable to complete separation?
To see why, let me explain what factor(year) actually does. When you write factor(year), R creates one binary indicator variable for each year in the dataset (minus a reference year). So if your data set spans 1960-2020, this would create 60 additional variables, 61 years minus one reference year. The 1987 dummy equals 1 for every country-year observation where year == 1987, and 0 otherwise. The 1988 dummy equals 1 only for observations in 1988, and so on.
Each dummy gets its own coefficient, capturing whether the probability of democracy differs in that year relative to the reference year, after accounting for the other predictors. But because this is a Markov transition model, that interpretation is conditional on the country having been autocratic in the previous year. So the coefficient on the 1987 dummy is effectively asking: “holding GDP and growth constant, were countries that had been autocratic more or less likely to become democratic in 1987 than in the reference year?”
To estimate that coefficient, the model needs variation in the outcome among observations where the dummy equals 1. Because the data are country-years, this means there must be at least some countries that remained autocratic (democracy = 0) and some that democratised (democracy = 1) among the countries observed in a given year.
Suppose that in 1987 some countries democratised while others remained authoritarian. Then the model can estimate a year effect by comparing those observations. But now imagine a year in which no country democratised. In that case, every observation where year == 1987 also has democracy = 0. Knowing the year tells us the outcome with certainty, meaning the 1987 dummy perfectly predicts the outcome.
This is what we mean by complete separation. The model no longer has enough information to estimate a reliable coefficient for that year dummy. Depending on how the optimiser handles the problem, the coefficient may be pushed toward extreme values or returned with an enormous standard error.
Continuous variables like l.log_gdppc rarely create this problem because they do not divide the data into perfectly separated groups. Per capita GDP varies across countries within each year, and countries with similar GDP levels can still differ in whether they democratise. The model therefore still has overlapping information from which to estimate a relationship.
Complete separation is therefore especially likely when a binary indicator variable aligns too neatly with a sparse binary outcome — exactly the risk created by year dummies in democracy-emergence models where transitions are rare and unevenly distributed across time.

There are two distinct warning signs to look for, which is why we run two separate checks.
First, we verify that the models are estimated on the same sample. While complete separation does not necessarily cause glm to drop observations, estimation problems can sometimes lead to effective differences in the estimation sample through omitted categories or failed coefficients. Comparing nobs() ensures that both specifications are fitted to the same set of observations:

# Check for dropped observations
nobs(emergence_no_fe)

[1] 4523

nobs(emergence_fe)

[1] 4523


The number of observations is the same in both models, so the fixed-effects specification is being estimated on the same sample as the model without year effects.
Second, even when observations are retained, complete separation often manifests through implausibly large standard errors on affected year dummies. We therefore inspect the year-fixed-effect coefficients directly:



Explanation of the Code

 
Line 1: summary(emergence_fe)$coefficients pulls out the coefficient table from the fitted model — a grid with one row per predictor and columns for the estimate, standard error, z/t value, and p value. Wrapping that in as.data.frame() turns the grid into a data frame, which is the format the next two lines need in order to pick out rows by name and refer to columns by name.
Line 2: This line narrows the table down to just the year dummies. Reading it from the inside out: rownames(coef_df) gets the name of every coefficient (e.g. "factor(year)2001", "gdp", etc.). grepl is a search function that goes through each name and flags whether the text factor(year) appears in it, returning TRUE for the year dummies and FALSE for everything else. So, grepl("factor\\(year\\)", rownames(coef_df)) searches exactly those names — the coefficient names we just pulled out — giving a TRUE/FALSE flag for each one. Finally, coef_df[..., ] uses those flags to keep only the flagged rows, leaving us with the year fixed effects and nothing else.
Line 3: This line sorts those year dummies by standard error and shows the worst offenders. Again from the inside out: order(-coef_df$Std. Error) works out the row order that puts the standard-error column from largest to smallest (the minus sign flips the default smallest-to-largest order). Wrapping the data frame in that ordering, coef_df[order(...), ], rearranges the rows so the biggest standard errors sit at the top. head(..., 10) then takes just the first 10 of those rows — the ten year dummies with the largest standard errors, which is exactly where signs of complete separation (implausibly huge standard errors) would show up first.



# Inspect year dummy standard errors for signs of separation
coef_df <- as.data.frame(summary(emergence_fe)$coefficients)
coef_df <- coef_df[grepl("factor\\(year\\)", rownames(coef_df)), ]
head(coef_df[order(-coef_df$`Std. Error`), ], 10)

If — as is the case here — the standard errors on the worst-affected year dummies run into the hundreds or thousands, this is strong evidence that complete separation is occurring and that the year effects are being estimated unreliably.
In this situation, the practical costs of including year fixed effects outweigh their theoretical benefits. Although the likelihood ratio test suggests that year effects contain explanatory information, the instability they introduce means the resulting estimates are not trustworthy. A common practice in the MTM literature is therefore to omit year fixed effects when they generate severe separation problems, while acknowledging the limitation and relying on clustered standard errors.
There are estimators designed specifically for cross-sectional dependence (your fellow-students on this module working with pooled OLS are using Driscoll-Kraay standard errors, for example), but they assume a linear model and a long time series. Since our rare-event binary MTM provides neither, we are unable to apply the same remedy here – country-clustered standard errors remain our best available correction.

An Overview of the Adjustments we have made
It is easy to confuse these methods because they all “adjust” the model, but they fall into two distinct jobs. Correcting bias in the coefficients, and correcting the uncertainty around the coefficients:

CRE (Correlated Random Effects): a bias fix. It removes omitted-variable bias by “soaking up” the stable, unobserved differences between countries (culture, geography, historical state capacity) that are correlated with your predictors.
Year Fixed Effects: also a bias fix, but for a different source. They absorb the “year-ness” of the data, filtering out global trends or crises that hit every country simultaneously – the cross-sectional dependence discussed just above, which clustering cannot address.
Clustered Standard Errors: an inference fix. These do not change your coefficients at all; they only correct the standard errors, so you do not overstate the precision of your results when observations within the same country are correlated over time.

So CRE and year fixed effects both belong on the bias side of the ledger – they differ only in whether the confounding comes from stable country traits or from common shocks in a given year – while clustered standard errors sit on the inference side. I have summarised this division of labour in Figure 1. You generally want all three, but as the year-fixed-effects discussion above showed, they must be implemented carefully – a correction that is sound in principle can still be infeasible in a particular dataset.
