title: Part II: Markov Transition Models with Correlated Random Effects
text:
Rationale
It is perfectly adequate to estimate the processes of democratic emergence and survival separately. There is a more elegant approach, however, in which emergence and survival are estimated together. This is the standard approach in the literature, but as you will see, it involves a lot of manual calculation and general faff which makes it prone to mistakes. One prominent example of such a mistake is in Przeworski et al. (2000)’s survival story. The authors claim that democracy is exogenous, meaning that it emerges for whatever reason but then gets sustained by economic development. The evidence for this claim stems partially from insignificant coefficients in their analysis for which they use the joint model we are about to discuss here. But as Epstein et al. (2006, p. 553) point out, Przeworski and his co-authors fail to report the correct significance test results for this joint estimation – casting doubt on their exogenous explanation of democratisation. Indeed, Boix & Stokes (2003) contest this finding and – using the same methodology correctly – show that democracy is in fact endogenous: it is itself a result of economic development. So, if this is so complicated that even seasoned academics get it wrong, why should we bother with this extra machinery?
The answer is not the coefficients themselves, as the point estimates from joint estimation are mathematically identical to what you would obtain by running separate models on the autocracy-year and democracy-year subsets. But the joint model has two important party-tricks up its sleeve that the separate models do not. First, it can tell us whether the effect of a variable differs statistically between emergence and survival. Secondly, it can assess whether the effect of a variable on democratic survival is itself statistically different from zero. To see how it does this, let’s have a look at its setup first.
The joint model fits a single equation across all observations, in which each independent variable is interacted with an indicator variable \(I_D\) (which is why this is also called an interaction model). This indicator variable is equal to the regime type in the previous year, \(y_{t-1}\). Hence, it will be equal to 1 if a country was a democracy in the previous year, and zero otherwise (notation adapted from Epstein et al. (2006, p. 553)). Following on from this, we can write the model as follows2:
\[
P(D_{i,t}) = \Phi(\beta_{0}+\beta_{1} X_{i,t-1} + \beta_{2} I_{D} + \beta_{3} I_{D} X_{i,t-1} + \epsilon_{i,t})
\tag{1}\]
where \(P(D_{it})\) is the probability that a country \(i\) was a democracy in year \(t\), \(\Phi\) is the cumulative normal distribution (the s-shaped distribution which you know from the introduction of probit in week 3), \(I_{D}\) the aforementioned indicator variable, \(X_{i,t-1}\) is an independent variable for country \(i\) in year \(t-1\), and \(\epsilon_{i,t}\) is a zero mean stochastic disturbance. I will drop \(\epsilon_{i,t}\) in what is to follow, as this is irrelevant for us here and now and I don’t want to confuse you unnecessarily.
As you have seen in Equation 1, this model is a multiplicative interaction model which allows us to model the probability of a country to be a democracy, conditional on its regime type in the previous year. The indicator variable \(I_{D}\), equal to \(y_{t-1}\) captures this information. How does this work?
Let us start by assuming that in year \(t-1\) country \(i\) was an autocracy. In this case, the indicator variable \(I_{D}\) would be equal to zero, and therefore Equation 1 can be re-written as
\[\begin{equation}
P(D_{i,t})=\Phi(\beta_{0}+\beta_{1} X_{i,t-1})
\end{equation}\]
In this case, the coefficient \(\beta_{1}\) would only represent the impact of variable \(X_{i,t-1}\) on the probability of an autocracy transitioning to democracy. Expressed more formally, we are dealing with conditional probabilities here, in the case of \(\beta_{1}\), we would obtain the impact of variable \(X_{i,t-1}\) on a country to be a democracy in year \(t\), under the condition that it was an autocracy in year \(t-1\). It is conditional on this, because we set the indicator variable to zero before.
We can construct a similar scenario for the condition, that a country was a democracy in the previous year. In this case, the indicator variable \(I_{D}\) would be equal to \(1\), and we would obtain Equation 1 again:
\[\begin{equation*}
P(D_{i,t})=\Phi(\beta_{0}+\beta_{1} X_{i,t-1} +\beta_{2} I_{D} + \beta_{3} I_{D} X_{i,t-1})
\end{equation*}\]
With \(I_{D}=1\), this can be simplified to:
\[\begin{equation}
P(D_{i,t})=\Phi((\beta_{0} +\beta_{2}) + (\beta_{1} + \beta_{3}) X_{i,t-1})
\end{equation}\]
This equation illustrates very well, that the impact of variable \(X_{i,t-1}\) on the probability of democracy to remain a democracy is now made up by the sum of the two coefficients \(\beta_{1}\) and \(\beta_{3}\), whereas the constant is the sum of coefficients \(\beta_{0}\) and \(\beta_{2}\).
With this knowledge in hand, we can return to the two party tricks a joint model is capable of. Firstly, it can tell us whether the effect of a variable differs between emergence and survival. This is the central element of the Przeworski–Boix debate: not whether development matters for emergence or survival in isolation, but whether it behaves differently in the two regimes. The interaction term \(\beta_3\) captures exactly the difference between the survival slope (\(\beta_1 + \beta_3\)) and the emergence slope (\(\beta_1\)), and its individual significance tells us whether the two processes are statistically distinguishable.
Secondly, a joint model can assess whether the effect of a variable on democratic survival is itself statistically different from zero. In the joint model, the survival slope is the sum \(\beta_1 + \beta_3\), and we cannot read its significance straight off the output — the p-value next to the interaction term tests \(\beta_3 = 0\), not \(\beta_1 + \beta_3 = 0\). We need a separate joint significance test for that sum. This is the test that takes us back to the critique I flagged at the start of this section. Przeworski et al. (2000) calculated the point estimates of the slope correctly3, but never performed the joint test of their significance (see Epstein et al., 2006). The joint model is the natural setting for this test, and avoiding the mistake is the second reason it is worth the extra machinery.
So, how should you use this in practice? For most other purposes — calculating predicted probabilities, drawing ROC curves, interpreting effects on each process — the separate models are easier to work with and give identical answers. But the joint model has some decided perks that make it worthwhile estimating. So the workflow I would recommend is:

estimate the joint model to (i) test whether emergence and survival are statistically distinguishable, and (ii) properly test the significance of the survival effect
then estimate emergence and survival separately and work with those models for everything else

title: Part II: Markov Transition Models with Correlated Random Effects
text:
Example
To make this more tangible, let’s look at an example. Assume we want to look at the effect of per capita GDP on democratic emergence (i.e. the transition of an autocracy to democracy), and democratic survival (i.e. the transition from democracy to democracy). Because we are using the CRE approach to control for unobserved heterogeneity, our model must include both the lagged variable and the country-specific mean, and both must be interacted with the regime indicator. In this case we would specify the model as follows:
\[\begin{align}
P(D_{i,t})=\Phi(& \beta_{0}+\beta_{1} \text{per capita GDP}_{i,t-1} +\beta_{2} I_{D} + \beta_{3} I_{D} \text{per capita GDP}_{i,t-1} + \\[0.6ex]
& \gamma_{1} \overline{\text{per capita GDP}}_{i} + \gamma_{2} I_{D} \overline{\text{per capita GDP}}_{i})
\end{align}\]
where \(\gamma_i\) are the coefficients for the between-country CRE baseline terms. The coefficient indicating the impact of per capita GDP on democratic emergence is \(\beta_{1}\). As illustrated above, the indicator variable \(I_{D}\) is zero in this case, and the equation would be reduced to
\[\begin{equation}
P(D_{i,t})=\Phi(\beta_{0}+\beta_{1} \text{per capita GDP}_{i,t-1} + \gamma_{1} \overline{\text{per capita GDP}}_{i})
\end{equation}\]
For democratic survival, the indicator variable \(I_{D}\) is one, and the coefficient indicating the impact of per capita GDP would be the sum of coefficients \(\beta_{1}\) and \(\beta_{3}\). Notice how the CRE control also shifts:
\[\begin{equation}
P(D_{i,t})=\Phi((\beta_{0} +\beta_{2}) + (\beta_{1} + \beta_{3}) \text{per capita GDP}_{i,t-1} + (\gamma_{1} + \gamma_{2}) \overline{\text{per capita GDP}}_{i})
\end{equation}\]

title: Part II: Markov Transition Models with Correlated Random Effects
text:
Application in R
How does all of this look in R, and how do you apply this to a real-world scenario? Let’s do this using the original example with properly lagged and logged per capita GDP in the global data set. You have already created the indicator variable \(I_{D}\) in the form of the variable l.democracy.
What we need next is a variable that captures \(I_{D} \text{per capita GDP}_{i,t-1}\), so that we can calculate \(\beta_{3}\). Furthermore, as just established mathematically, we also need to interact our country-specific mean (mean_log_gdppc) with the indicator variable to calculate \(\gamma_2\). This allows the structural effect of a country’s average wealth to behave differently in dictatorships versus democracies.

# Interaction for the within-country effect
world$l.log_gdppc_l.democracy <- world$l.democracy * world$l.log_gdppc

# Interaction for the between-country (CRE) effect
world$mean_log_gdppc_l.democracy <- world$l.democracy * world$mean_log_gdppc

Now, we are ready to estimate the model. Remember, formally, the core of the model is written as:
\[\begin{align}
P(D_{i,t}) = \Phi(& \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} \text{log(per capita GDP)}_{i,t-1} + \beta_{2} I_{D} + \beta_{3} I_{D} \text{log(per capita GDP)}_{i,t-1} + \\[0.6ex]
& \gamma_{1} \overline{\text{log(per capita GDP)}}_{i} + \gamma_{2} I_{D} \overline{\text{log(per capita GDP)}}_{i})
\end{align}\]
We replace this in the R command with the equivalent variables, making sure to include our two Mundlak mean_ terms at the end to purge the unobserved country bias:

joint <- glm(democracy ~ l.log_gdppc + l.democracy + l.log_gdppc_l.democracy + 
                         mean_log_gdppc + mean_log_gdppc_l.democracy, 
             data = world,
             na.action = na.exclude,
             family = binomial(link = "probit"))


If you have done regression analysis before, and you worry about (multi-)collinearity in such a model, then please note that:

Analysts should include all constitutive terms when specifying multiplicative interaction models except in very rare circumstances. By constitutive terms, we mean each of the elements that constitute the interaction term. Thus, X and Z are the constitutive terms in [this model: \(y=\beta_0 + \beta_1 X + \beta_2 Z + \beta_4 XZ + \epsilon\)]. (Brambor et al., 2006, p. 66)

If you do not know about this problem, yet, then you will do so after next week.

You should obtain the following output:

summary(joint)

Standard Errors in Joint Estimation
Just as with the separate emergence and survival models, the joint model has the same panel structure — many years of data per country — and we therefore need to cluster the standard errors by country for the same reasons outlined in the Section on Standard Errors. We calculate the clustered variance-covariance matrix once, and then use it both to display the coefficient table with clustered SEs and to perform the joint significance test:

library(lmtest)
library(sandwich)

joint_vcov <- vcovCL(joint, cluster = ~ countrycode, type = "HC3")

coeftest(joint, vcov. = joint_vcov)

For democratic emergence, we can report the Intercept (Intercept) and the slope coefficient l.log_gdppc straight away as -1.989 and 0.0120005, respectively. The slope is essentially zero and statistically insignificant (\(p \approx 0.759\)): for autocracies, per capita GDP appears to have no effect on the probability of transitioning to democracy. This is in line with the findings from estimating emergence separately. But lets now turn to the party tricks of the joint model I discussed in the introduction to this section.


The Joint Model’s Party Tricks Applied
The first trick is to assess whether the effect of GDP differs between emergence and survival. This is read directly off the interaction term \(\beta_3\), here l.log_gdppc_l.democracy. The coefficient is large (0.28) and highly significant (\(1.4328 \times 10^{-03}\)), which tells us that yes, the effect of GDP on the probability of democracy in year \(t\) depends substantially on whether the country was a democracy in year \(t-1\). This is the comparison the separate models cannot make, and it is consistent with the pattern Przeworski et al. predicted: development behaves differently in the two regimes.
The second party trick is to show us the actual effect of GDP on democratic survival, and to indicate whether it is significantly different from zero. The survival slope is the sum \(\beta_1 + \beta_3\), and substantively this gives us the effect of GDP among countries that were already democracies. To get the point estimate, we add l.log_gdppc and l.log_gdppc_l.democracy. But for statistical significance we cannot simply read it off the output – the p-value next to l.log_gdppc_l.democracy tests whether \(\beta_3\) alone is zero, not whether the sum \(\beta_1 + \beta_3\) is zero. To test the latter, we need a joint test that uses the covariance between \(\beta_1\) and \(\beta_3\). This is the mistake Przeworski et al. (2000) made, as discussed in the first few pages of Epstein et al. (2006): they did not use the results of this joint test.
For the joint test of whether the survival slope \(\beta_1 + \beta_3\) is significantly different from zero, we use linearHypothesis() from the car package, which lets us pass the same clustered vcov in directly:

library(car)
joint_test <- linearHypothesis(
  joint,
  "l.log_gdppc + l.log_gdppc_l.democracy = 0",
  vcov. = joint_vcov,
  test = "Chisq"
)

joint_test

Model 1: restricted model
Model 2: democracy ~ l.log_gdppc + l.democracy + l.log_gdppc_l.democracy + 
    mean_log_gdppc + mean_log_gdppc_l.democracy

With p \(5.5175 \times 10^{-05}\) we can reject the null hypothesis that the survival slope \(\beta_1 + \beta_3\) is zero, and conclude that per capita GDP helps explain democratic survival.

Could the p-values differ?
The value of the survival slopes (the point estimates) are unaffected by separate or joint estimation, they will be identical. But can the joint test and the separate model’s significance test produce different p-values? The answer is yes, and in panel data with clustered standard errors, the difference can be noticeable. The two tests are evaluated against different variance-covariance matrices. The joint Wald test uses the full-sample clustered vcov, where each country’s cluster spans both its autocracy-years and democracy-years. The separately-estimated survival model only sees democracy-years, so the within-country observation structure differs and the HC3 small-sample correction is calculated from a different estimating sample. The two p-values typically agree closely, but they need not be identical, and the joint test is the conceptually correct one when the question is about the survival slope as the sum \(\beta_1 + \beta_3\).



Model Fit with Joint Estimation
Despite all of this extra work around the joint estimation, you will be delighted to hear that no extra calculation of the ROC curve is required. Why? The joint model produces exactly the same predicted probabilities, provided the joint and separate models are estimated on the same observations – autocracy-year predictions match what emergence gives us, and democracy-year predictions match what survival gives us. Since the ROC curve is built entirely from predicted probabilities compared against observed outcomes, a ROC for the joint model would be identical to the union of the two separate ROCs. There is no additional information to gain. The joint model exists to answer questions about statistical significance — whether the effect of a variable differs across regimes, and whether the survival slope is itself significant — both of which require the joint variance-covariance matrix. For predictive fit, the separate models give us everything we need.

title: Part II: Markov Transition Models with Correlated Random Effects
text:
How to Measure Model Fit
There are quite a few model fit measures around for binary response models, such as pseudo R-Squared and the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC). What I am going to present here, however, is the so-called ROC curve, as I personally really don’t like the aforementioned measures.

What is it?
The principle idea of ROC is to show how good a model is at distinguishing democracies from dictatorships when we vary the decision threshold used to turn predicted probabilities into classifications. It approaches this question by comparing the actual observed values of the dependent variable with the values the model would predict, given the values of the independent variables.

ROC Curve
A graphical measure of model fit for binary outcome models, constructed by plotting the True Positive Rate (TPR) against the False Positive Rate (FPR) across all possible classification thresholds \(\tau\). A model with no predictive power traces the diagonal (TPR = FPR), whilst a model with perfect separation produces a curve that reaches the upper-left corner. The further the curve lies above the diagonal, the better the model distinguishes between the two categories of the dependent variable.

Consider Figure 2 a). On the x-axis you see eight observations, marked as coloured circles. Red circles represent countries which are dictatorships, and orange ones democracies. They are sorted by their respective level of per capita GDP. Now suppose that these are predicted probabilities from a model we have estimated. With a cut off point \(\tau=0.5\) we would correctly predict the group of four observations on the left to be dictatorships. They are True Negative (TN). The group on the right would be correctly predicted as democracies, these are True Positive (TP). We have no incorrectly classified cases; our model has been able to separate cases perfectly. You can see this represented in the form of distributions in panel b).
   






Figure 2: Perfect Separation



   
As you well know by now, the real world is oddly deficient in achieving perfection such as this. We will observe both poor democracies, and rich dictatorships. This scenario is shown in Figure 3 a).
   






Figure 3: Overlap



According to the CDF we would predict the poor democracy as a dictatorship. It would be a False Negative (FN). Conversely, we would predict the rich dictatorship as a democracy and would obtain a False Positive (FP).

True and False Positives and Negatives
The four possible outcomes when comparing a model’s predicted classification against the observed outcome. A True Positive (TP) occurs when the model correctly predicts a positive outcome (e.g. democracy). A True Negative (TN) occurs when it correctly predicts a negative outcome (e.g. dictatorship). A False Positive (FP) occurs when the model predicts a positive outcome that is not observed, and a False Negative (FN) occurs when it predicts a negative outcome for a case that is in fact positive.

The distribution of cases in Figure 3 b) is not as clearly separated any more as in Figure 2 b). Now they overlap, leading to incorrect classifications. These are marked accordingly in Figure 4. As we are no longer operating in a world in which we only have TNs and TPs, I think we can all agree that our model fit is no longer as good as in Figure 2.






Figure 4: False Negatives and False Positives



But there is another issue: whilst setting \(\tau\) at 0.5 makes intuitive sense, there is nothing preventing us from shifting \(\tau\) around. Indeed, the number of FPs and FNs very much depends on where we place our cut-off point. For example, if we don’t want any FNs, then we just have to shift \(\tau\) sufficiently downwards. Or if we want to avoid FPs we only need to move it far enough upwards. I have illustrated this in Figure 5 a) and b), respectively.






Figure 5: Shifting \(\tau\)



These are only three options of placing the threshold. But we have a total of eight observations which means that there are nine potential positions for the cut-off point with each leading to a different conclusion of how well our model fits the observed data. Let’s go through this more systematically and start by placing \(\tau\) at the very bottom. Because the number of TNs, TPs, FNs, and FPs will only change at the “next” observation we only need to shift as many times as there are observations. For each shift we record the values of all four quantities in a crosstabulation which is displayed in the following table:

These tables are useful in their own right, but since we will end up with as many of them as there are observations, this can quickly get very messy. There are only eight observations here, but imagine doing these for the world data set with 190 observations… We therefore need to find a way to condense the information contained in each of the n confusion matrices into a single measure. If you look closely, you will see that TNs and FPs form a close relationship: if we shift up \(\tau\) in Figure 5 a) we are reducing the number of FPs and obtain more TNs. As TPs relate in the same way to FNs, we can quantify their respective relationships in the following rates:
\[\begin{equation}
\text{False Positive Rate}=1-\text{Specificity}=\frac{\text{False Positives}}{\text{False Positives}+\text{True Negatives}}
\end{equation}\]
 
In our case you can think of the False Positive Rate (FPR) as the proportion of incorrectly specified dictatorships.
\[
\begin{align}
\text{True Positive Rate}=\text{Sensitivity}&=\frac{\text{True Positives}}{\text{True Positives}+\text{False Negatives}}\\[10pt]
\text{Specificity}
&= \frac{\text{True Negatives}}{\text{True Negatives} + \text{False Positives}}
= 1 - \text{False Positive Rate} \nonumber
\end{align}
\]
 
For our example the True Positive Rate (TPR) represents the proportion of correctly specified democracies.

True Positive Rate and False Positive Rate
Summary statistics derived from a confusion matrix. The True Positive Rate (TPR, also called sensitivity) is the proportion of actual positive cases correctly predicted as positive: \(\text{TPR} = \frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP} + \text{FN}}\). The False Positive Rate (FPR) is the proportion of actual negative cases incorrectly predicted as positive: \(\text{FPR} = \frac{\text{FP}}{\text{FP} + \text{TN}}\). These two rates are plotted against one another across all thresholds to produce the ROC curve.

If we calculate these rates for each of our n confusion matrices, we are already reducing four quantities into two. Let’s do it. To provide a visual aid in this rather laborious process, I have created Figure 6 which depicts all eight shifts.

We are nearly there! The last step is to display all these values in the form of a curve with the TPR on the y-axis, and the FPR on the x-axis. You can see the result – the ROC curve – in Figure 7 a).
 






Figure 7: ROC Curve



Note that I have added a diagonal where TPR = FPR. This is sometimes described as a model without independent variables. I like to think of the line as the graphical point where our model would not be able to separate between the two categories, at all. The further the ROC curve is away from the diagonal, the better our model is at separating the two categories. But there are two sides to the diagonal. We want it to be above the diagonal, as here the model is predicting 0s as 0s and 1s as 1s. Underneath, the prediction is inverse and 0s are predicted as 1s, and 1s are predicted as 0s.
To summarize the position of the curve into a numerical expression, the area under the curve (AUC) is used, as shown in Figure 7 b). If the area is 100% we are correctly predicting everything. At 50% the model is incapable of separation, and at 0% the model gets everything wrong. This is very useful to compare different models.

Area Under the Curve (AUC)
A scalar summary of the ROC curve, equal to the area beneath it, and bounded between 0 and 1. An AUC of 1 indicates perfect classification, an AUC of 0.5 indicates a model with no predictive power (equivalent to random guessing), and an AUC below 0.5 indicates a model that systematically predicts the wrong category. AUC values are particularly useful for comparing the fit of competing models on the same data.



R
How do you do all of this in R? Let’s start with the simple emergence model. In order to calculate a ROC curve, we need a new package, called pROC. Install it and load it.

library(pROC)

To calculate the ROC curve, we need a few steps:

prob_em <- predict(emergence, type = "response")

world_democ0$prob_em <- unlist(prob_em)

roc1 <- roc(world_democ0$democracy, world_democ0$prob_em)

auc(roc1)

What does each line do?

add the vector prob_em to the data frame world_democ0. In order to do this, we need to unlist the values in the prob_em vector.
we then call the roc function in which we compare the predicted probabilities (world_democ0$prob_em) with the actual, observed regime type (world_democ0$democracy) and store the result in an object called roc
as a last step we calculate the area under the curve with the auc() function

But we can also plot the ROC curve:

Note that print.auc = TRUE prints the numerical value into this plot. You can suppress it by setting it to FALSE.

text:
The Super-Honest Table
If you want to stop here (in terms of modelsummary, that is), then you have my blessing for the assessment. The results, as reported in Table 4 are perfectly acceptable. However, the pedants amongst you will have noticed that the standard errors for the survival models in Table 4 stem from estimating emergence and survival separately. Since these can differ in joint estimation, a super-honest results table will have to carry out this joint estimation, calculate clustered standard errors, and then perform the Wald-Test we calculated above for each survival model. And this is where the code becomes complex. I have annotated it, and divided it into sections (well, Claude did that) which I will explain in more detail below the table. I will also give you some instructions on how to change this code if you want to use it for your assessment – it is not as difficult as it might at first seem. But here we go:
 


library(modelsummary)
library(pROC)
library(tinytable)
library(sandwich)
library(car)
library(tibble)
library(dplyr)

# ============================================================
# 1. ESTIMATE THE FOUR SEPARATE MODELS (CRE Updated)
# ============================================================

emergence <- glm(democracy ~ l.log_gdppc + mean_log_gdppc, 
                 data = world_democ0, 
                 na.action = na.exclude,
                 family = binomial(link = "probit"))

emergence_full <- glm(democracy ~ l.log_gdppc + l.life + l.enrol_gross + 
                                  mean_log_gdppc + mean_life + mean_enrol_gross, 
                      data = world_democ0, 
                      na.action = na.exclude,
                      family = binomial(link = "probit"))

survival <- glm(democracy ~ l.log_gdppc + mean_log_gdppc,
                data = world_democ1, 
                na.action = na.exclude,
                family = binomial(link = "probit"))

survival_full <- glm(democracy ~ l.log_gdppc + l.life + l.enrol_gross +
                                 mean_log_gdppc + mean_life + mean_enrol_gross,
                     data = world_democ1, 
                     na.action = na.exclude,
                     family = binomial(link = "probit"))

# ============================================================
# 2. ESTIMATE THE TWO JOINT MODELS (Classical and New)
# ============================================================
# The joint model fully interacts each IV with l.democracy.
# This makes the joint-model point estimates equivalent to the
# separately-estimated emergence and survival coefficients,
# while pooling the variance information across both subsets.

joint_classical <- glm(democracy ~ (l.log_gdppc + mean_log_gdppc) * l.democracy, 
                       data = world,
                       na.action = na.exclude,
                       family = binomial(link = "probit"))

joint_new <- glm(democracy ~ (l.log_gdppc + l.life + l.enrol_gross + 
                              mean_log_gdppc + mean_life + mean_enrol_gross) * l.democracy,
                 data = world,
                 na.action = na.exclude,
                 family = binomial(link = "probit"))

# Clustered vcovs for the joint models
vcov_joint_classical <- vcovCL(joint_classical, 
                               cluster = ~ countrycode, type = "HC3")

vcov_joint_new <- vcovCL(joint_new, 
                         cluster = ~ countrycode, type = "HC3")

# ============================================================
# 3. EXTRACT JOINT-MODEL SEs FOR THE SURVIVAL SLOPES
# ============================================================
# DO NOT TOUCH THIS SECTION
# For each variable X, the survival slope is β_X + β_{X:l.democracy}.
# Its variance is Var(β_X) + Var(β_{X:l.democracy}) + 2*Cov(...).

joint_se <- function(joint_model, joint_vcov, var_name) {
  # Construct a contrast vector that picks out the survival slope
  # for variable `var_name`: 1 for the main effect, 1 for the
  # interaction with l.democracy.
  coefs <- coef(joint_model)
  interaction_name <- paste0(var_name, ":l.democracy")
  
  contrast <- rep(0, length(coefs))
  names(contrast) <- names(coefs)
  contrast[var_name]         <- 1
  contrast[interaction_name] <- 1
  
  # SE of the linear combination
  sqrt(t(contrast) %*% joint_vcov %*% contrast) |> as.numeric()
}

joint_coef <- function(joint_model, var_name) {
  coefs <- coef(joint_model)
  interaction_name <- paste0(var_name, ":l.democracy")
  as.numeric(coefs[var_name] + coefs[interaction_name])
}

# Survival intercept: (Intercept) + l.democracy
joint_intercept_se <- function(joint_model, joint_vcov) {
  coefs <- coef(joint_model)
  contrast <- rep(0, length(coefs))
  names(contrast) <- names(coefs)
  contrast["(Intercept)"] <- 1
  contrast["l.democracy"] <- 1
  sqrt(t(contrast) %*% joint_vcov %*% contrast) |> as.numeric()
}

joint_intercept_coef <- function(joint_model) {
  coefs <- coef(joint_model)
  as.numeric(coefs["(Intercept)"] + coefs["l.democracy"])
}

# ============================================================
# 4. PATCH THE SURVIVAL MODEL OBJECTS WITH JOINT-DERIVED SEs
# ============================================================
# We build vcov matrices for the survival models in which the
# diagonal entries are the joint-model variances of the linear
# combinations (β + β_interaction), and the off-diagonals are
# extracted analogously. modelsummary will then square-root the
# diagonals to display the joint-derived SEs.

build_survival_vcov <- function(survival_model, joint_model, joint_vcov) {
  surv_coefs <- names(coef(survival_model))
  n <- length(surv_coefs)
  V <- matrix(0, n, n, dimnames = list(surv_coefs, surv_coefs))
  
  # Build a matrix of contrasts: each row picks out the linear
  # combination from the joint model that corresponds to that
  # coefficient in the separate survival model.
  contrasts <- matrix(0, nrow = n, ncol = length(coef(joint_model)),
                      dimnames = list(surv_coefs, names(coef(joint_model))))
  
  for (cf in surv_coefs) {
    if (cf == "(Intercept)") {
      contrasts[cf, "(Intercept)"] <- 1
      contrasts[cf, "l.democracy"] <- 1
    } else {
      interaction_name <- paste0(cf, ":l.democracy")
      contrasts[cf, cf]               <- 1
      contrasts[cf, interaction_name] <- 1
    }
  }
  
  # Full vcov of the linear combinations: contrasts %*% V_joint %*% t(contrasts)
  V <- contrasts %*% joint_vcov %*% t(contrasts)
  V
}

# Build the joint-derived vcov matrices for the survival models
vcov_survival_joint      <- build_survival_vcov(survival,      joint_classical, vcov_joint_classical)
vcov_survival_full_joint <- build_survival_vcov(survival_full, joint_new,       vcov_joint_new)

# Sanity check: the joint-derived survival coefficients should match
# the separately-estimated ones to machine precision.
# Quick check (uncomment to verify):
# coef(survival)["l.log_gdppc"]
# joint_coef(joint_classical, "l.log_gdppc")

# ============================================================
# 5. ASSEMBLE THE VCOV LIST FOR modelsummary
# ============================================================
# Emergence columns use the standard cluster-robust vcov.
# Survival columns use the joint-derived vcov calculated above.

vcov_list <- list(
  "Cluster-Robust" = vcovCL(emergence,      cluster = ~ countrycode, type = "HC3"),
  "Cluster-Robust" = vcovCL(emergence_full, cluster = ~ countrycode, type = "HC3"),
  "Cluster-Robust" = vcov_survival_joint,
  "Cluster-Robust" = vcov_survival_full_joint
)

# ============================================================
# 6. PREDICTED PROBABILITIES AND ROC CURVES (unchanged)
# ============================================================

world_democ0$prob_classical <- unlist(predict(emergence,      type = "response"))
world_democ0$prob_new       <- unlist(predict(emergence_full, type = "response"))
world_democ1$prob_classical <- unlist(predict(survival,       type = "response"))
world_democ1$prob_new       <- unlist(predict(survival_full,  type = "response"))

roc1 <- roc(world_democ0$democracy, world_democ0$prob_classical)
roc2 <- roc(world_democ0$democracy, world_democ0$prob_new)
roc3 <- roc(world_democ1$democracy, world_democ1$prob_classical)
roc4 <- roc(world_democ1$democracy, world_democ1$prob_new)

# AUC row
rows <- tibble(
  `~term` = "AUC (ROC)",
  `~(1)`  = as.numeric(auc(roc1)),
  `~(2)`  = as.numeric(auc(roc2)),
  `~(3)`  = as.numeric(auc(roc3)),
  `~(4)`  = as.numeric(auc(roc4))
)
attr(rows, "position") <- 10

# ============================================================
# 7. COEFFICIENT LABELS
# ============================================================

cm <- c(
  'l.log_gdppc'   = 'per capita GDP (logged, lagged)',
  'l.life'        = 'Life Expectancy (lagged)',
  'l.enrol_gross' = 'Gross Primary Enrollment (lagged)',
  '(Intercept)'   = 'Intercept'
)

# ============================================================
# 8. RESULTS TABLE
# ============================================================

modelsummary(
  list(
    "Classical" = emergence,
    "New"       = emergence_full,
    "Classical" = survival,
    "New"       = survival_full
  ),
  vcov      = vcov_list,
  estimate  = "{estimate}{stars}",
  statistic = "({std.error})",
  gof_omit  = 'DF|Deviance|Log.Lik|F|AIC|BIC|RMSE',
  coef_map  = cm,
notes = c(
    "+ p < 0.1, * p < 0.1, ** p < 0.05, *** p < 0.01",
    "Standard errors are cluster-robust (HC3), clustered by country.",
    "Models include country-specific averages (Correlated Random Effects) to control for unobserved heterogeneity. These coefficients are omitted from the table for clarity.",
    "Survival columns: standard errors derived from the fully-interacted joint model, accounting for the covariance between the emergence slope (β₁) and the interaction (β₃)."
  ),
  add_rows  = rows
) |>
  group_tt(j = list("Emergence" = 2:3, "Survival" = 4:5)) |>
  group_tt(j = list("Dependent Variable:<br>Democracy" = 2:5))

I don’t think I promised too much when I said this was going to be complex. This is the most ambitious block of code on the entire module, so let me walk you through it section by section. Don’t worry if the matrix algebra in the middle looks intimidating – you don’t need to understand the mathematical details to use the code. What matters is knowing what each section is for, so you can adapt it to your own analysis.
Section 1: Estimate the four separate models
Nothing new here. We estimate the four models — Classical and New versions for both emergence and survival — exactly as we did earlier in the chapter. These are the models whose coefficients appear in the table.
Section 2: Estimate the two joint models
This is the first new piece. We estimate two additional probit models — one for the Classical specification (just GDP) and one for the New specification (GDP, life expectancy, and gross enrolment). Both are estimated on the full dataset, not on the autocracy-year or democracy-year subsets.
The crucial detail is the formula. In the Classical version, we write democracy ~ l.log_gdppc * l.democracy. The asterisk is R shorthand: it tells R to include the main effect of l.log_gdppc, the main effect of l.democracy, and the interaction between them. In the New version, we wrap all three independent variables in brackets and multiply the whole bracket by l.democracy, which produces all three main effects, the l.democracy dummy, and one interaction term per independent variable.
This is what we called a fully-interacted joint model above. Crucially, the coefficients from these joint models reproduce exactly the coefficients you would get by running separate emergence and survival models — the joint model is just a different way of expressing the same information.
We then calculate clustered variance-covariance matrices for both joint models using vcovCL(), exactly as we did for the four separate models.
Section 3: Helper functions
This section defines three small utility functions. You can think of them as little tools that the next section will use.
The first, joint_coef(), calculates the survival slope for a given variable by adding \(\hat{\beta}_1\) (the emergence effect) and \(\hat{\beta}_3\) (the interaction) from the joint model. If you give it a variable name like "l.log_gdppc", it returns the survival slope that would correspond to that variable.
The second, joint_se(), calculates the standard error of that same survival slope, using the joint model’s variance-covariance matrix. The maths behind it is the subject of the bulb callout just below – for now, the important thing is that the function does the right calculation behind the scenes.
The third and fourth helpers do the same thing for the intercept, since the survival intercept in the joint model is the sum \(\beta_0 + \beta_2\) (where \(\beta_2\) is the coefficient on l.democracy).
You don’t need to understand the matrix multiplication inside these functions. The important thing is: these are the tools that translate the joint model’s output into the survival-slope quantities we want for the table.

Why the off-diagonals matter here
Remember the variance-covariance matrix from the discussion in Standard Errors in Markov Transition Models? We noted then that its off-diagonal entries fade into the background most of the time, but matter the moment you ask a question about a combination of coefficients. This is that moment. The survival slope is the sum \(\hat{\beta}_1 + \hat{\beta}_3\). Its variance follows the general rule for the variance of a sum: \(\text{Var}(A + B) = \text{Var}(A) + \text{Var}(B) + 2\,\text{Cov}(A, B)\). The factor of 2 appears because \(\text{Cov}(A, B)\) and \(\text{Cov}(B, A)\) both contribute and are equal — these are exactly the symmetric off-diagonal entries you saw schematically in the discussion in Standard Errors in Markov Transition Models. So the SE of the survival slope is not simply \(\sqrt{\text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_1) + \text{Var}(\hat{\beta}_3)}\); it requires the covariance from the off-diagonal too. The helper function joint_se() does exactly this calculation behind the scenes: it constructs a contrast vector picking out the two relevant coefficients, then calculates the SE of their sum using the full vcov including the off-diagonals. The off-diagonals are quietly carrying the analytical weight here.

Section 4: Build the survival vcov matrices
This is the most technical-looking section, but the goal is simple: we want to construct a variance-covariance matrix for each survival model that looks like the one we’d get from running vcovCL() on survival, but whose numbers actually come from the joint model instead.
The function build_survival_vcov() does this by setting up what’s called a contrast matrix — basically, a table that says “to get the survival slope for l.log_gdppc, take the main effect plus the interaction.” It does this for every variable in the survival model, including the intercept. The resulting matrix is then transformed using the joint model’s vcov to give us a survival-specific vcov whose diagonal entries are the joint-derived variances and whose off-diagonal entries are the joint-derived covariances.
Don’t get hung up on the maths. What’s happening at a conceptual level is that we’re saying: “Instead of calculating the survival model’s standard errors from the survival-year subset alone, calculate them from the joint model that uses both subsets and accounts for the covariance between emergence and survival effects.”
We then call this function twice — once for the Classical survival model, once for the New survival model — producing two new vcov matrices.
Section 5: Assemble the vcov list
The vcov_list is the list modelsummary consumes to know which standard errors to display for each model. Earlier we passed in four cluster-robust vcovs, one per separate model. Now we still pass in four, but for the survival columns we pass in our joint-derived vcovs instead of the ones calculated on the survival subset alone.
The emergence columns are unchanged. Only the survival columns get the joint treatment.
Sections 6–8: Predicted probabilities, AUC, labels, and the table
These sections are essentially unchanged from before. We calculate predicted probabilities, calculate ROC curves and AUCs, build the AUC row that gets appended to the table, set up the coefficient labels, and then call modelsummary() with the updated vcov_list.
One thing has changed in the table call: there’s a third note at the bottom explaining that the survival-column standard errors come from the joint model, and that the point estimates are still identical to what you would get from estimating the survival model separately. This is the honest disclosure: readers can see at a glance that the table mixes two estimation approaches, and they can read the note for the rationale.
 

What if you want to adapt this for your own analysis?
The code above is built around the specific example this week — four models in total, two for emergence and two for survival — but the structure is general. You can adapt it for your own regional dataset, your own theoretical approach, and as many or as few models as your argument needs. Below is a section-by-section guide. Work through it in order, since later sections depend on the choices you make in earlier ones. I will take you through the adjustments in an abstract way first, but will then also take you through a concrete example.
Section 1: The separate models. This section estimates the individual emergence and survival models. You will need to make several decisions:

Replace world_democ0 and world_democ1 with your own regional equivalents — your dataset filtered to l.democracy == 0 and l.democracy == 1 respectively. Make sure you have created l.democracy first, using group_by(country) and mutate(l.democracy = lag(democracy)), exactly as we did at the start of this week’s material.
Decide which independent variables you want. The example uses three: l.log_gdppc, l.life, and l.enrol_gross. Your assessment may use different ones — perhaps l.log_gdppc and l.gdppc_growth for Classical Modernisation, with health or education variables added for New Modernisation. Or different variables altogether if you are testing Dependency Theory, the resource curse, or cultural explanations.
Decide how many models you want. The example has two specifications per process (Classical and New), giving four models total. You may want more — perhaps three nested specifications building up in complexity, or competing variants within the same theoretical tradition. Add as many glm() calls as you need, but try to add them in pairs: one emergence model and one matching survival model. This keeps the column groupings in the final table clean. If you only want an emergence model without a survival counterpart (or vice versa), the code will still work, but you will need to think carefully about how the “Emergence” and “Survival” headers in the final table line up.


A practical note: tables with more than five or six columns get hard to read on a portrait page. If you find yourself wanting more, consider whether two separate tables (one for emergence, one for survival) might serve your argument better than one wide one, or whether some specifications could move to a robustness appendix.

Section 2: The joint models. You need one joint model for each distinct variable set used in the separate models. In the example, all the Classical specifications use just l.log_gdppc, and all the New specifications use the same three IVs, so two joint models suffice. If you have, say, three nested Classical specifications that use progressively more variables, you need three joint models — one matching the variable set of each separate specification.
The pattern is: for every separate emergence model with variables \(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_k\), there is a joint model democracy ~ (X_1 + X_2 + ... + X_k) * l.democracy whose point estimates reproduce both that emergence model and its matching survival model. So:

For each unique variable set across your separate models, write one joint glm() call.
For single-variable specifications, you can drop the brackets: democracy ~ l.log_gdppc * l.democracy.
For multi-variable specifications, wrap the IVs in brackets: democracy ~ (l.log_gdppc + l.gdppc_growth + l.life) * l.democracy. The brackets matter — without them, R will not generate the interaction terms you need.
calculate a clustered vcov for each joint model with vcovCL().

Sections 3 and 4: The helper functions and the survival vcov. These sections contain the matrix algebra. They work for any number of variables and any number of models — the functions read the coefficients out of the joint model automatically. Do not touch Section 3.
What you do need to do in Section 4 is build a survival vcov for each of your survival models. This means that there needs to be one build_survival_vcov() call for each survival model. In the example we have two: vcov_survival_joint and vcov_survival_full_joint. If you have three survival models, you need three build_survival_vcov() calls.
Section 5: Assemble the vcov list. This is where the most coordination is needed. The vcov_list must contain one entry per model, in exactly the same order as the models will appear in the modelsummary() call in Section 8. For emergence models, use the standard vcovCL() output. For survival models, use the joint-derived vcov you built in Section 4.
Section 6: Predicted probabilities and ROC curves. Add one predict() call and one roc() call per model. The naming convention in the example pairs each prediction with the dataset it lives in (predictions for emergence models go in world_democ0, predictions for survival models in world_democ1), and assigns each ROC object a number (roc1, roc2, …). Follow the same pattern, however many models you have.
Section 7: Coefficient labels. Update the coef_map to match every variable that appears in any of your models. The variable names on the left of the = must be exactly the names as they appear in your glm() formulas; the right side is whatever human-readable label you want to display in the table (see Stimson, n.d.).

cm <- c(
  'l.log_gdppc'    = 'per capita GDP (logged, lagged)',
  'l.gdppc_growth' = 'GDP Growth (lagged)',
  'l.life'         = 'Life Expectancy (lagged)',
  'l.enrol_gross'  = 'Gross Primary Enrollment (lagged)',
  '(Intercept)'    = 'Intercept'
)

Any coefficient not listed in coef_map will be silently dropped from the table – so if a variable is mysteriously missing from your output, this is the first place to check.
Section 8: The results table. Several things to attend to here, especially if you have changed the number of models:

Update the list() inside modelsummary() to include all your models, in the order you want them to appear. Use the column-header labels you want displayed (e.g. "Classical" = emergence).
Expand the add_rows tibble to include one AUC entry per model column. Each column gets its own ~(N) entry, where N is the column number.
Update the group_tt() column ranges. The example uses 2:3 for Emergence and 4:5 for Survival because there are two models on each side. If you have three emergence models and two survival models, your column ranges become 2:4 for Emergence and 5:6 for Survival. Count carefully — the first column (column 1) is the coefficient labels, not a model.
The order of the vcov_list entries (from Section 5) must match the order of the models in the modelsummary() call. Do not shuffle one without shuffling the other — if they fall out of sync, the table will silently display the wrong standard errors with no error message to warn you. The same applies to the AUC entries in add_rows: they must be in the same order as the models in the table.
Adjust the AUC row position. The line attr(rows, "position") <- 10 places the AUC row at position 10 — just below the observation count. If you add or remove independent variables, the number of rows above the AUC will change, and you will need to update this number. The simplest way to find the right value: render the table once with attr(rows, "position") <- 1, see where the AUC row appears, and shift it downward until it lands where you want it (just below “Num.Obs.” but above the GOF statistics is the standard location).

One sanity check before you trust the output. After running all the sections, verify that the joint models are producing the same point estimates as the separate models. Run:

# These should match
coef(survival)["l.log_gdppc"]
joint_coef(joint_classical, "l.log_gdppc")

These two numbers should be identical to several decimal places. Repeat the check for each variable in each survival model, paired with the appropriate joint model. If anything fails to match, the most likely culprit is that the joint model has dropped observations the separate models retained (or vice versa), because of missing values in different variables. Check the sample sizes with nobs(survival) and nobs(joint_classical) — if they differ in ways you can’t explain, something is off. Get in touch with me so we can look at it together.

To make this a little more tangible, I have rewritten the code to incorporate three models for emergence and survival, respectively. joint_se <- function(joint_model, joint_vcov, var_name) {

# ============================================================
# 4. JOINT-DERIVED VCOVs FOR SURVIVAL MODELS
# ============================================================

# DO NOT TOUCH THESE FUNCTIONS

build_survival_vcov <- function(survival_model, joint_model, joint_vcov) {
  surv_coefs  <- names(coef(survival_model))
  joint_full  <- coef(joint_model)
  joint_coefs <- names(joint_full)[!is.na(joint_full)]

  needed <- character(0)
  for (cf in surv_coefs) {
    needed <- c(needed,
                if (cf == "(Intercept)") c("(Intercept)", "l.democracy")
                else c(cf, paste0(cf, ":l.democracy")))
  }
  missing <- setdiff(needed, joint_coefs)
  if (length(missing) > 0) {
    stop("joint model dropped coefficient(s): ", paste(missing, collapse = ", "),
         ". Inspect summary(joint_model).")
  }

  n <- length(surv_coefs)
  contrasts <- matrix(0, nrow = n, ncol = length(joint_coefs),
                      dimnames = list(surv_coefs, joint_coefs))
  for (cf in surv_coefs) {
    if (cf == "(Intercept)") {
      contrasts[cf, "(Intercept)"] <- 1; contrasts[cf, "l.democracy"] <- 1
    } else {
      contrasts[cf, cf] <- 1; contrasts[cf, paste0(cf, ":l.democracy")] <- 1
    }
  }
  V <- contrasts %*% joint_vcov %*% t(contrasts)

  # Guard: fail clearly here rather than deep inside modelsummary
  if (!all(is.finite(V)) || any(diag(V) < 0)) {
    stop("Non-finite or negative variance in derived survival vcov — ",
         "joint model is likely near-singular for this specification.")
  }
  V
}

Note that the within term enters lagged (l.log_gdppc), whereas the Mundlak mean is taken over the unlagged series (mean(log_gdppc)). Strictly, the country mean should be the time-average of the regressor that actually appears in the model, but over a country’s full time series the lagged and unlagged means differ only by a single endpoint observation, so the distinction is immaterial here. The mean’s role is to soak up the stable between-country component, and that component is unchanged by shifting the series one year.↩︎

title: Introduction
text:
VIF in Fixed Effects Models
Things become slightly more involved when we move from a pooled model to a fixed effects model. The reason is that car::vif() does not have a dedicated method for plm objects, and even if we coerce it to work, it would calculate the VIFs on the raw, un-demeaned regressors. This is not what we want. Recall that a fixed effects model relies on the within transformation: each variable is expressed as a deviation from its country (or unit) mean, so that only variation within a country over time identifies the coefficients. Multicollinearity in an FE model is therefore a question about the demeaned regressors, not the original ones. A variable that varies a lot across countries but barely within them will look perfectly well-behaved in a pooled VIF, yet may be near-collinear once the country means are subtracted.
To obtain a meaningful VIF for the FE specification, we exploit the fact that a within (FE) model is numerically equivalent to an OLS regression that includes a dummy variable for each country. This is known as the least-squares dummy variable (LSDV) representation. Once we estimate the model in this form using lm(), we can apply vif() directly:

# LSDV-equivalent of the FE model
lsdv_model <- lm(polity5 ~ log_gdppc_lag1 + life_lag1 + enrol_gross_lag1 +
                   factor(countrycode),
                 data = df)
vif(lsdv_model)

                        GVIF Df GVIF^(1/(2*Df))
log_gdppc_lag1      7.508232  1        2.740115
life_lag1           8.612889  1        2.934772
enrol_gross_lag1    2.651699  1        1.628404
factor(countrycode) 7.918452 18        1.059162


Because the model contains a factor variable (countrycode) with many levels, car::vif() does not return a single VIF per regressor. Instead, it returns what is called a generalised variance inflation factor (GVIF), along with the degrees of freedom of each term and a third column, GVIF^(1/(2*Df)). The output is therefore organised into three columns.
The first column, GVIF, reports the generalised variance inflation factor for each term. For terms with a single degree of freedom — here, our three substantive regressors — this number is identical to a conventional VIF and can be read directly against the familiar thresholds of 5 and 10. The second column, Df, indicates the degrees of freedom occupied by each term: one for each of our lagged covariates, and 18 for factor(countrycode) (i.e. 19 countries minus the reference category). The first column is not directly comparable across terms with different degrees of freedom, which is why the third column, GVIF^(1/(2*Df)), exists: it rescales the GVIF onto a common scale so that terms of different dimensionality can be compared directly. To apply our conventional thresholds to this column, we compare against \(\sqrt{5} \approx 2.24\) and \(\sqrt{10} \approx 3.16\).
One word of caution on interpretation: the row corresponding to factor(countrycode) will typically display a large GVIF. This is expected and not a substantive concern. The country dummies are not regressors of theoretical interest; they exist solely to absorb the country fixed effects. In our output, the rescaled value of 1.06 in fact tells us that, once we account for the high dimensionality of the term, the fixed effects are not unduly collinear with our covariates — reassuring, since it confirms that meaningful within-country variation remains in the substantive regressors after demeaning.
What we care about, then, are the GVIFs of our three substantive variables. log_gdppc_lag1 has a VIF of 7.51, and life_lag1 a VIF of 8.61. Both sit between the conventional thresholds of 5 and 10, indicating a moderate-to-high degree of multicollinearity. This is not surprising — log GDP per capita and life expectancy are strongly correlated empirically, as richer countries tend to have longer-lived populations, and the two variables are partly capturing the same underlying dimension of development. enrol_gross_lag1, with a VIF of 2.65, is well below both thresholds and poses no concern.
Whether the collinearity between log_gdppc_lag1 and life_lag1 constitutes a problem depends on which threshold we adopt. Under the stricter threshold of 5, both variables would be flagged; under the more permissive threshold of 10, neither would. In practice this is a judgement call. If both variables are theoretically essential to the model, we would simply report the VIFs transparently and acknowledge that the standard errors of these two coefficients are somewhat inflated. If one of them is dispensable, dropping it would yield more precise estimates of the remaining coefficient — though at the cost of omitted-variable bias if the dropped variable genuinely belongs in the model.

VIF in FE Models
You only need to estimate an lsdv_model model to run the vif() test. Otherwise, you can stick to the code I introduced you to last week.

section: What should you do if you find evidence for (multi-)collinearity?
text:
What should you do if you find evidence for (multi-)collinearity?
On the face of it, the solution does appear simple: drop one of the affected variables. But this is also where it starts getting difficult. Which of the two (or three) should you drop? Or should you not do anything, at all?
Perhaps somewhat surprisingly, the advisable option is usually the latter. If all of the variables you are including are required by the theory you are testing, then leaving one of them out – for whatever reason – can cause Omitted Variable Bias (OVB). In this case, you would resolve collinearity, but at the price of causing another, potentially more serious problem. So, it is usually preferable to accept the collinearity problem in a model, and to make sure that you test your theory properly.
But you should test for this problem nonetheless, and be honest about it in any research project. Should (multi-) collinearity be an issue, you can refer back to it as one of the many possible explanation why certain coefficients may be insignificant. This can be done either in the analysis section directly, or in the discussion.

Exercises
These exercises use the world.csv to put the methods you learned about last week to work on all three democratisation mechanisms we cover on this module: modernisation, dependency, and the resource curse.
This is the first time you put these methods into practice yourself, rather than reading about them. Every exercise follows the same arc – fit the models, read the output R hands back, and turn that output into a substantive claim about democracy. The fitting becomes routine soon enough; the part that takes real practice, and the part that earns marks in the assessment, is the reading and the interpreting – working out what the columns of coefficients are actually telling you, and noticing when they are quietly telling you something false.
What changes from one exercise to the next is which stage of that arc takes centre stage:
The three models are not interchangeable; each was chosen because it contains a little surprise that the others do not. So, as you work through these, watch less for whether a result is significant and more for where the estimate moves from one column to the next, and why – that movement is where this week’s methodological lesson actually lives.

title: Part I: Country Fixed Effects Models with Driscoll-Kraay Standard Errors
text:
Setting Up
Run this once at the top of your script. It loads the packages, builds the lagged predictors, and declares a separate panel for each exercise (dropping missing values, which vcovSCC() will not tolerate).

library(tidyverse)
library(plm)
library(lmtest)
library(modelsummary)

# Load data
df <- read.csv("world.csv")

# Create log GDP per capita
df <- df |> mutate(log_gdppc = log(gdppc))

# Lagged predictors, within country. Most use a 1-year lag; natural resource
# rents use a 5-year lag (see the note in Exercise 2).
df <- df |>
  arrange(countrycode, year) |>
  group_by(countrycode) |>
  mutate(
    log_gdppc_lag1  = dplyr::lag(log_gdppc,  1),
    life_lag1       = dplyr::lag(life,       1),
    agri_lag1       = dplyr::lag(agri,       1),
    natural_lag5    = dplyr::lag(natural,    5),
    oil_lag1        = dplyr::lag(oil,        1),
    v2x_neopat_lag1 = dplyr::lag(v2x_neopat, 1)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

# Years with adequate coverage
df_panel <- df |> filter(year >= 1995 & year <= 2019)

# One panel per exercise, NAs dropped on that exercise's variables only
pdata_1 <- pdata.frame(na.omit(df_panel[, c("countrycode","year","polity5",
                       "log_gdppc_lag1","life_lag1")]),
                       index = c("countrycode","year"))
pdata_2 <- pdata.frame(na.omit(df_panel[, c("countrycode","year","polity5",
                       "agri_lag1","natural_lag5","log_gdppc_lag1")]),
                       index = c("countrycode","year"))
pdata_3 <- pdata.frame(na.omit(df_panel[, c("countrycode","year","polity5",
                       "oil_lag1","v2x_neopat_lag1","log_gdppc_lag1")]),
                       index = c("countrycode","year"))


Why 1995–2019?
The V-Dem variables have meaningful coverage from the mid-1990s. The five-year lag on natural resource rents reaches back to 1990, by which point the World Bank rent data are also available. Capping at 2019 avoids the COVID-19 disruption.

title: Part I: Country Fixed Effects Models with Driscoll-Kraay Standard Errors
section: Exercise 1: From OLS to pooled OLS to fixed effects (Modernisation)
text:
Exercise 1: From OLS to pooled OLS to fixed effects (Modernisation)
Modernisation theory holds that development – wealth and the human capital that comes with it – makes democracy more likely. We will test it with lagged log GDP per capita and lagged life expectancy: the simplest model in the worksheet, and the right one to learn the machinery on.
This first exercise is a guided walk. We add one piece at a time and stop after each to look at what changed. Run each block, read the output, and read the note that follows before moving on.

Step 1 — Plain OLS
Start where Week 2 left off: an ordinary regression that treats every country-year as a separate, independent observation.

ols_1 <- lm(polity5 ~ log_gdppc_lag1 + life_lag1, data = pdata_1)
coeftest(ols_1)

Read off the two coefficients and their significance. Both are positive and both are starred, which looks like clean support for modernisation theory. Hold onto those two numbers – the rest of the exercise is about watching them, and the confidence we attach to them, change.


Step 2 — Pooled OLS with Driscoll-Kraay standard errors
Now re-estimate exactly the same model with plm(), and attach the Driscoll-Kraay correction.

pooled_1 <- plm(polity5 ~ log_gdppc_lag1 + life_lag1,
                data = pdata_1, model = "pooling")

dk_1 <- vcovSCC(pooled_1, type = "HC3", cluster = "time")

coeftest(pooled_1, vcov = dk_1)

Put this output next to Step 1 and look carefully. The coefficients have not moved at all – the same two numbers you noted a moment ago. What has changed is the standard error column, and with it the t-statistics and p-values. This is the first of the two moments: correcting for the fact that a country’s score this year is tied to its score last year changes how confident we are in an estimate, not the estimate itself.
If you want to see why the coefficients were always going to stay put, print the correction itself:

dk_1                 # the Driscoll-Kraay matrix the SEs come from
sqrt(diag(dk_1))     # square-root its diagonal — exactly the SEs in your output

The standard errors are simply the square roots of the numbers running down the diagonal of that matrix. vcovSCC() rebuilds the matrix; it never touches the coefficients, which were fixed by the regression itself.


Step 3 — Fixed effects with Driscoll-Kraay standard errors
Finally, switch the estimator from "pooling" to "within" to add country fixed effects, and recompute the correction for the new model.

fe_1 <- plm(polity5 ~ log_gdppc_lag1 + life_lag1,
            data = pdata_1, model = "within", effect = "individual")

dk_fe_1 <- vcovSCC(fe_1, type = "HC3", cluster = "time")

coeftest(fe_1, vcov = dk_fe_1)

Compare the GDP coefficient with the one you have been carrying since Step 1. This time the coefficient itself has changed – it is noticeably smaller. That is the second moment, and it is a different kind of change from Step 2. Fixed effects stop asking “are richer countries more democratic?” and start asking “when a country grows richer, does it become more democratic?”, and the two questions need not have the same answer.
You now have the whole pipeline in front of you, and the two lessons that sit at the heart of this part of the module: moving from plain to pooled OLS changes your confidence in an estimate; moving to fixed effects can change the estimate itself. The exercises that follow take each of these moves and push on it – to show that the standard errors do not always move the way you would guess, and that the coefficients sometimes move dramatically.


Reflection Questions

Between Step 1 and Step 2 the coefficients did not change but the standard errors did. In your own words, why does correcting the standard errors leave the coefficients untouched? (If it helps, refer to the matrix you printed: which part of it became the standard errors, and which part of the model produced the coefficients?)
In Step 3 the coefficient on GDP per capita dropped once country fixed effects were added. Fixed effects compare each country to its own history rather than to other countries. What does that drop suggest about how much of the plain-OLS income–democracy association was really “wealthy countries differ in other ways too” rather than “growing richer makes a country more democratic”?

Exercise 2: Predict, then check (Dependency)
Dependency theory argues that reliance on primary-commodity exports entrenches underdevelopment and weak governance – the opposite of the modernisation story. You will test it with agri (agriculture as a share of GDP) and natural (total resource rents), controlling for income.

Why natural is lagged five years. Agriculture’s share of GDP moves slowly with structural change, so a one-year lag suffices. Resource rents, by contrast, swing sharply with global commodity prices; a one-year lag would mostly capture price noise rather than the structural dependence the theory is about. Following Ross (2001), natural is lagged five years, isolating the slow institutional channel – eroded taxation, patronage, a hollowed-out civil society – through which resource wealth is said to damage governance.

Before you read on or touch R, commit to predictions. Fill in each cell with a sign (+/−) and whether you expect significance, and guess which way Driscoll-Kraay will push each standard error:

ols_2    <- lm(f2, data = pdata_2)
pooled_2 <- plm(f2, data = pdata_2, model = "pooling")

coeftest(ols_2)
coeftest(pooled_2, vcov = vcovSCC(pooled_2, type = "HC3", cluster = "time"))
coeftest(fe_2,     vcov = vcovSCC(fe_2,     type = "HC3", cluster = "time"))


Reflection Questions

You almost certainly predicted a negative sign for agriculture in both columns – that is what dependency theory says. Check them. The pooled and fixed-effects estimates disagree, and not just in size but in sign. Explain how the cross-national answer and the within-country answer can point in opposite directions, and say which of the two is the one that actually supports dependency theory.
Natural-resource rents spring two surprises at once: Driscoll-Kraay makes the standard error smaller, and fixed effects shrink the coefficient roughly tenfold. Take them separately. Why can an honestly-computed standard error come out below the naive one? And what does the FE shrinkage mean once you remember that the within-country variation in rents is mostly global price cycles, not changes in dependence?
Given that agriculture’s sign flips between the two estimators, how confident can you be that agricultural dependence causes lower democracy? Describe one within-country story that would produce a negative FE coefficient with no dependency mechanism involved at all.

title: Part I: Country Fixed Effects Models with Driscoll-Kraay Standard Errors
text:
Exercise 3: Diagnose the model (Resource Curse)
Now you are the sceptical reader. The resource-curse model – oil rents and neopatrimonialism (v2x_neopat, capturing personalised, clientelistic rule), controlling for income – is the the most complex of the three, and it contains three traps that a careless analyst, reading only one column, would fall straight into. Run the pipeline, then find them.

f3 <- polity5 ~ oil_lag1 + v2x_neopat_lag1 + log_gdppc_lag1

ols_3    <- lm(f3, data = pdata_3)
pooled_3 <- plm(f3, data = pdata_3, model = "pooling")
fe_3     <- plm(f3, data = pdata_3, model = "within", effect = "individual")

dk_3    <- vcovSCC(pooled_3, type = "HC3", cluster = "time")
dk_fe_3 <- vcovSCC(fe_3,     type = "HC3", cluster = "time")

coeftest(ols_3)
coeftest(pooled_3, vcov = dk_3)
coeftest(fe_3,     vcov = dk_fe_3)


Reflection Questions

Oil’s coefficient is large and rock-solid across both cross-sectional columns, then very nearly vanishes under fixed effects, clinging to a single significance marker. What does that collapse say about whether the resource curse is a dynamic within countries or a stable feature of which countries happen to have oil? And what, if anything, is left of a causal claim once you note that the within-country variation in rents is largely price-driven?
With neopatrimonialism in the model, income’s coefficient turns negative in the cross-section, then flips back positive under fixed effects. Explain the cross-sectional sign by thinking about the kind of country that is both very rich and firmly undemocratic, and why the within-country comparison tells a different story.
Neopatrimonialism is about as slow-moving as a political variable gets, so the textbook prediction is that fixed effects estimate it poorly. Instead its coefficient grows. What within-country comparison is the FE estimator making here, and why does that comparison sharpen this particular effect rather than blur it?


Read the v2x_neopat coefficient with care
Notice what sits on each side of the regression. The dependent variable, Polity V, is built largely around constraints on the executive – the checks a legislature and judiciary place on the chief executive. But v2x_neopat is itself constructed from sixteen indicators that include executive respect for the constitution, judicial independence, legislative oversight, and the autonomy of the electoral body – and its Presidentialism sub-index explicitly captures how far the president is free from constraints by other institutions.
In other words, the regressor and the outcome are partly measuring the same thing – executive constraint – from opposite directions. This is a construct validity problem: a large negative coefficient is partly definitional rather than causal, because an unconstrained executive counts as both “more neopatrimonial” and “less democratic” almost by construction. No lag and no clustered standard error fixes this, because the overlap is in the concepts themselves, not in the error term.
Two further worries sit on top, and unlike the construct overlap these are genuine endogeneity (see lecture slides of Week 3): the independent variable is entangled with the error term, not merely with how the outcome is defined. The causal arrow plausibly runs both ways – personalised rule erodes democracy, but weak democracy also lets clientelism and corruption flourish (reverse causality, or simultaneity when both happen at once) – and because both series barely move from year to year, the one-year lag only partly separates them.
Therefore, treat v2x_neopat as a control that soaks up institutional context, not as a variable whose coefficient you interpret. The variable you are actually testing here is oil.

    "Plain OLS"     = ols_3,
    "Pooled DK"     = pooled_3,
    "Fixed Effects" = fe_3
  ),
  vcov  = list(NULL, dk_3, dk_fe_3),   # plain OLS keeps its own SEs
  stars = TRUE,
  fmt   = 3,
  coef_rename = c(
    "oil_lag1"        = "Oil rents % GDP (lag 1)",
    "v2x_neopat_lag1" = "Neopatrimonialism index (lag 1)",
    "log_gdppc_lag1"  = "Log GDP per capita (lag 1)"

  gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared", "adj.r.squared"),
  notes = c(

The NULL in the vcov list tells modelsummary to leave the plain-OLS column on its own naive standard errors. That is deliberate – the whole point of the table is to show a reader exactly what moves when you switch to the corrected errors, so the columns must not be silently harmonised.


Reflection Questions

Track oil’s significance stars across the three columns (*** → *** → a lone +). What would a reader who saw only the plain-OLS column conclude, and – in one sentence – why is that conclusion wrong?
The fixed-effects \(R^2\) (0.289) sits well below the pooled \(R^2\) (0.575), but the two are not measuring the same thing. Explain what the within \(R^2\) counts, and what the gap between the two figures tells you about whether the variation in democracy lives mostly between countries or within them over time.
Write the two-to-three-sentence methods note that justifies Driscoll-Kraay over plain OLS to a non-specialist reader – without using the words “variance-covariance matrix” or “heteroscedasticity”.

Synthesis

Across the worksheet you have watched fixed effects reverse a sign (agriculture), gut a coefficient (oil), and inflate others (life expectancy, neopatrimonialism), while Driscoll-Kraay mostly left significance intact. In two or three sentences, say where the consequential surprises in this module actually came from – the standard-error correction or the choice of estimator – and what that implies for where you should spend your attention when you analyse your own panel.
Life expectancy and neopatrimonialism are both slow-movers, yet both survived fixed effects here. Does that mean the slow-mover worry is overblown? title: Part II: Markov Transition Models with Correlated Random Effects
text:
Exercises
These exercises build a Markov Transition Model one piece at a time and put it to work on on all three democratisation mechanisms we cover on this module: modernisation, dependency, and the resource curse. We will use the world dataset. The dependent variable throughout is democracy (1 = democracy, 0 = autocracy) by Miller et al. (2022).
This is the first time you fit these models yourself rather than read about them. The fitting becomes routine quickly; the skill these exercises develop is reading the output – and in particular telling apart two things a static model cannot separate at all: whether income (or oil, or commodity dependence) helps democracies emerge, or helps them survive.
What changes from one exercise to the next is which part of that work takes centre stage:
crumbs: 13  Part II: Markov Transition Models with Correlated Random Effects

title: Part II: Markov Transition Models with Correlated Random Effects
text:
Setting Up
Run the following before beginning. It loads the packages, creates all the lagged variables and the country-specific means used for the Correlated Random Effects (CRE) models, and builds the two subsets the MTM needs.

library(tidyverse)
library(pROC)

# Load data
world <- read.csv("world.csv")

# Log GDP per capita
world <- world |> mutate(log_gdppc = log(gdppc))

# Create all lagged variables AND the country means within each country.
# The means are the Mundlak/CRE terms; they must be computed across the full
# panel, before the data are split into transition states.
world <- world |>
  arrange(country, year) |>
  group_by(country) |>
  mutate(
    # Lagged variables
    l.democracy     = lag(democracy),
    l.log_gdppc     = lag(log_gdppc),
    l.gdppc_growth  = lag(gdppc_growth),
    l.agri          = lag(agri),
    l.natural       = lag(natural),
    l.oil           = lag(oil),
    l.v2x_neopat    = lag(v2x_neopat),

    # Country means (CRE terms), taken over the unlagged series
    mean_log_gdppc    = mean(log_gdppc,    na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_gdppc_growth = mean(gdppc_growth, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_agri         = mean(agri,         na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_natural      = mean(natural,      na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_oil          = mean(oil,          na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_v2x_neopat   = mean(v2x_neopat,   na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

# Subsets for the MTM
world_democ0 <- filter(world, l.democracy == 0)   # was autocracy last year
world_democ1 <- filter(world, l.democracy == 1)   # was democracy last year


Why lag the independent variables?
Lagging the dependent variable is a methodological requirement of the MTM – we need last year’s regime type to condition this year’s probability on it. Lagging the independent variables is a substantive choice: it is reasonable to assume the economy or institutions in year \(t-1\) shape the regime outcome in year \(t\), rather than the two being settled simultaneously. That distinction is worth stating clearly in your methods section.
