title: Part II: Markov Transition Models with Correlated Random Effects
section: Exercise 1: From a static probit to a Markov Transition Model (Modernisation)
text:
Exercise 1: From a static probit to a Markov Transition Model (Modernisation)
Modernisation theory predicts that development promotes democracy. We test it with the two simplest predictors – lagged log GDP per capita and lagged GDP growth – and the right model to learn the machinery on. This exercise is a guided walk: we add one piece at a time and stop after each to see what it bought us. Run each block, read the output, and read the note before moving on.

Step 1 — A static probit
Start where the cross-sectional weeks left off: a probit that treats every country-year as an independent observation.

probit_1 <- glm(democracy ~ l.log_gdppc + l.gdppc_growth,
                data = world, na.action = na.exclude,
                family = binomial(link = "probit"))
summary(probit_1)

Income is positive and strongly significant – this reads like clean support for modernisation theory. Note the coefficient on l.log_gdppc; we will watch it the whole way through.


Step 2 — Add last year’s regime
Regime type is sticky: most country-years look like the year before. Add last year’s regime as a predictor.

probit_ldv <- glm(democracy ~ l.log_gdppc + l.gdppc_growth + l.democracy,
                  data = world, na.action = na.exclude,
                  family = binomial(link = "probit"))
summary(probit_ldv)

The income coefficient drops sharply. Last year’s regime is by far the strongest predictor of this year’s, and a good deal of what income looked like it was doing was really standing in for regime persistence. But notice the catch built into this model: l.democracy applies the same adjustment whether a country was a democracy or an autocracy last year – as if escaping autocracy and holding on to democracy were the same problem. They are not, and that tension is exactly what the next step resolves.


Step 3 — Split the process: the Markov Transition Model
Instead of one model with a lagged-regime term, estimate two models on the two starting points. Democratic emergence (countries that were autocracies last year):

emergence_1 <- glm(democracy ~ l.log_gdppc + l.gdppc_growth,
                   data = world_democ0, na.action = na.exclude,
                   family = binomial(link = "probit"))
summary(emergence_1)

Democratic survival (countries that were democracies last year):

survival_1 <- glm(democracy ~ l.log_gdppc + l.gdppc_growth,
                  data = world_democ1, na.action = na.exclude,
                  family = binomial(link = "probit"))
summary(survival_1)

This is the heart of the week. Each process now has its own intercept and its own coefficients, free to differ – and they do. Compare the income coefficient across the two models: it is a very different thing for whether an autocracy becomes a democracy than for whether a democracy stays one. A single pooled model can never show you this.


Step 3b — Guard against unobserved heterogeneity (CRE)
The lagged coefficients so far mix two things: how a country differs from other countries, and how it changes relative to its own past. To isolate the second, add each country’s long-run mean of the predictors – the Mundlak/CRE terms from the setup chunk.

emergence_1_cre <- glm(democracy ~ l.log_gdppc + l.gdppc_growth +
                         mean_log_gdppc + mean_gdppc_growth,
                       data = world_democ0, na.action = na.exclude,
                       family = binomial(link = "probit"))
summary(emergence_1_cre)

survival_1_cre <- glm(democracy ~ l.log_gdppc + l.gdppc_growth +
                        mean_log_gdppc + mean_gdppc_growth,
                      data = world_democ1, na.action = na.exclude,
                      family = binomial(link = "probit"))
summary(survival_1_cre)

The mean_ terms are nuisance terms – their only job is to soak up stable between-country differences, and we never interpret them. What they leave behind in the lagged coefficients is the cleaner within-country effect. Watch the survival income coefficient move once its mean is included: part of what it carried was between-country, and the mean has now taken it. From here on we work with these CRE specifications.


Step 4 — Honest standard errors
The CRE models still report default standard errors that assume every observation is independent. They are not: a country’s observations are correlated over time. Cluster the standard errors by country to allow for that.

library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)

coeftest(emergence_1_cre,
         vcov. = vcovCL(emergence_1_cre, cluster = ~ countrycode, type = "HC3"))

coeftest(survival_1_cre,
         vcov. = vcovCL(survival_1_cre, cluster = ~ countrycode, type = "HC3"))

The coefficients do not change – only the standard errors, and the t-statistics and p-values that follow from them. Two details matter and will not change again for the rest of the worksheet. We pass the cluster as a one-sided formula, cluster = ~ countrycode, rather than a vector: glm() silently drops missing rows, so a vector pulled from the data frame could be the wrong length, whereas the formula lets vcovCL() re-derive the clusters from the exact sample the model was fitted on. And we use type = "HC3" rather than the more common HC1 because, with only around 170 countries, the cluster count is moderate rather than large, and HC3 applies a more conservative small-sample correction that downweights influential clusters.


Step 5 — How well does each model fit?
Finally, ROC curves and their AUCs for the static probit, the LDV probit, and the two CRE models.

prob_p1 <- predict(probit_1, type = "response")
world$prob_p1 <- unlist(prob_p1)
roc_p1 <- roc(world$democracy, world$prob_p1); auc(roc_p1)

prob_ldv <- predict(probit_ldv, type = "response")
world$prob_ldv <- unlist(prob_ldv)
roc_ldv <- roc(world$democracy, world$prob_ldv); auc(roc_ldv)

prob_em1 <- predict(emergence_1_cre, type = "response")
world_democ0$prob_em1 <- unlist(prob_em1)
roc_em1 <- roc(world_democ0$democracy, world_democ0$prob_em1); auc(roc_em1)

prob_sur1 <- predict(survival_1_cre, type = "response")
world_democ1$prob_sur1 <- unlist(prob_sur1)
roc_sur1 <- roc(world_democ1$democracy, world_democ1$prob_sur1); auc(roc_sur1)

The AUC leaps when you add last year’s regime – unsurprisingly, since regime type barely changes year to year. The survival model scores high and the emergence model barely beats a coin toss, and the reason is not that one model is “better”: it is that breakdowns are rare and transitions are rarer still, so the two are very different prediction problems. Keep that in mind before reading any AUC as a verdict on a theory.
You have now built the whole pipeline, and seen its payoff: the emergence/survival split, which lets income matter for one process and not the other. The exercises that follow stop rebuilding it and start pushing on it.


Reflection Questions

Between Step 1 and Step 2 the coefficient on income roughly halved when last year’s regime entered the model. What does l.democracy absorb, and why does adding it pull income down?
The LDV in Step 2 gives every country the same adjustment for last year’s regime; the MTM in Step 3 instead estimates emergence and survival as two separate models. In your own words, why is that separation the right move for studying regime change – what can the two-model version see that the single-coefficient version cannot?
Survival is far easier to predict than emergence (compare the two AUCs). Explain why, in terms of how often democracies break down versus how often autocracies make the leap.



Going further (optional): do years matter?
Clustering handles correlation within countries over time. A different worry is correlation across countries in the same year – a global wave of democratisation, a worldwide recession. Year fixed effects are the standard fix. Use a likelihood-ratio test to see whether they are jointly significant, then look hard at the fitted dummies before trusting them.

library(lmtest)

emergence_no_fe <- glm(democracy ~ l.log_gdppc + l.gdppc_growth,
                       data = world_democ0, na.action = na.exclude,
                       family = binomial(link = "probit"))
emergence_fe    <- glm(democracy ~ l.log_gdppc + l.gdppc_growth + factor(year),
                       data = world_democ0, na.action = na.exclude,
                       family = binomial(link = "probit"))
lrtest(emergence_no_fe, emergence_fe)

# Are any year dummies wildly imprecise? (a sign of separation)
coef_df <- as.data.frame(summary(emergence_fe)$coefficients)
coef_df <- coef_df[grepl("factor\\(year\\)", rownames(coef_df)), ]
head(coef_df[order(-coef_df$`Std. Error`), ], 10)

Repeat for the survival subset. The point of the exercise is not to add the dummies but to discover why you cannot: in years with no transitions (emergence) or no breakdowns (survival), a year dummy perfectly predicts the outcome and its coefficient cannot be estimated. Recognising that, and saying so, is part of responsible applied work.

title: Part II: Markov Transition Models with Correlated Random Effects
text:
Exercise 2: Predict, then check (Dependency)
Dependency theory predicts that reliance on primary commodities suppresses democracy. We use l.agri (agriculture as a share of GDP, a proxy for structural commodity dependence) and l.natural (total natural resource rents), controlling for income. You know the pipeline now, so we go straight to the CRE models – but first, commit to predictions.
Before you run anything, fill in what dependency theory leads you to expect:
 










Variable
Emergence: sign & significant?
Survival: sign & significant?




l.natural




l.agri







 
And one harder prediction, which is really the point of the exercise: if resource dependence does hold democracy back, where in the CRE model will that show up – in the lagged within-country term l.natural, or in the country mean mean_natural?
Now estimate. The static probit is worth a glance for the raw signs; the CRE MTM and the clustered standard errors are where you check your predictions.

# Raw signs
probit_2 <- glm(democracy ~ l.agri + l.natural + l.log_gdppc,
                data = world, na.action = na.exclude,
                family = binomial(link = "probit"))
summary(probit_2)

# CRE MTM
emergence_2_cre <- glm(democracy ~ l.agri + l.natural + l.log_gdppc +
                         mean_agri + mean_natural + mean_log_gdppc,
                       data = world_democ0, na.action = na.exclude,
                       family = binomial(link = "probit"))
survival_2_cre  <- glm(democracy ~ l.agri + l.natural + l.log_gdppc +
                         mean_agri + mean_natural + mean_log_gdppc,
                       data = world_democ1, na.action = na.exclude,
                       family = binomial(link = "probit"))

# Honest standard errors, exactly as in Exercise 1
coeftest(emergence_2_cre, vcov. = vcovCL(emergence_2_cre, cluster = ~ countrycode, type = "HC3"))
coeftest(survival_2_cre,  vcov. = vcovCL(survival_2_cre,  cluster = ~ countrycode, type = "HC3"))


Reflection Questions

You almost certainly predicted that l.natural would be negative and significant – the resource curse, operating within countries over time. Check it. The significant negative resource term is not the lagged one at all; it is the country mean, mean_natural, in the emergence model. Explain what it means substantively that the curse shows up between countries but not within a country from one year to the next.
Look at l.log_gdppc in the survival model and compare it with what you found in Exercise 1, where income clearly carried survival. Once commodity dependence is in the specification, does income still protect survival? What does that say about how robust the Exercise 1 finding really was?
The emergence model rests on only about a hundred actual transitions, and the CRE means spend further degrees of freedom on that thin subset. How should that shape how cautiously you read its coefficients and their significance?

title: Part II: Markov Transition Models with Correlated Random Effects
text:
Exercise 3: Diagnose the model (Resource Curse)
The resource-curse hypothesis predicts that oil wealth suppresses democracy. We test l.oil and l.v2x_neopat (neopatrimonialism – the degree of personalised, clientelistic rule), controlling for income. Now you are the sceptical examiner. Estimate the models, then find the three places where a careless reading would go wrong.

# Raw signs
probit_3 <- glm(democracy ~ l.oil + l.v2x_neopat + l.log_gdppc,
                data = world, na.action = na.exclude,
                family = binomial(link = "probit"))
summary(probit_3)

# CRE MTM
emergence_3_cre <- glm(democracy ~ l.oil + l.v2x_neopat + l.log_gdppc +
                         mean_oil + mean_v2x_neopat + mean_log_gdppc,
                       data = world_democ0, na.action = na.exclude,
                       family = binomial(link = "probit"))
survival_3_cre  <- glm(democracy ~ l.oil + l.v2x_neopat + l.log_gdppc +
                         mean_oil + mean_v2x_neopat + mean_log_gdppc,
                       data = world_democ1, na.action = na.exclude,
                       family = binomial(link = "probit"))

coeftest(emergence_3_cre, vcov. = vcovCL(emergence_3_cre, cluster = ~ countrycode, type = "HC3"))
coeftest(survival_3_cre,  vcov. = vcovCL(survival_3_cre,  cluster = ~ countrycode, type = "HC3"))


Reflection Questions

Oil’s only significant term anywhere in the two models is the country mean, mean_oil, in the emergence model – the lagged l.oil is not significant in either. What does that tell you about whether the oil–autocracy link is a within-country dynamic (a country pumping more oil becomes less democratic) or a stable feature of which countries have oil in the first place?
The familiar resource-curse story expects oil and neopatrimonialism to block democratic emergence. Instead, the term that reaches significance is neopatrimonialism in the survival model, and it does not significantly predict emergence. Read that carefully: what real-world process does a significant negative neopatrimonialism coefficient in the survival model describe, and why is it close to the opposite of what the standard story would have led you to predict?
In Exercise 1 income clearly carried survival; here it is marginal at best once oil and neopatrimonialism are in the model. Taken with the same pattern you saw in Exercise 2, what does this teach you about reading any single coefficient – including a headline one – in isolation from the rest of the specification?


Read the v2x_neopat coefficient with care
The dependent variable here is the Boix–Miller–Rosato measure, which is deliberately minimalist: a country counts as a democracy if its executive is elected and accountable, its legislature is chosen in free and fair elections, and a majority of adult men can vote. It says nothing about what happens between elections. v2x_neopat, by contrast, is built from sixteen indicators of clientelism, presidential dominance, and corruption [vdem:2025]. So there is little overlap between the two measures – no serious construct validity problem – and a country can clear the BMR bar while remaining deeply neopatrimonial, which is exactly why the variable is worth including.
Even so, the coefficient is best read as an association, not a clean causal effect. With no real construct overlap to worry about here, the threat that remains is endogeneity (see lecture slides of Week 3): the independent variable ends up correlated with the error term because the causal arrow plausibly runs both ways. Crossing the electoral threshold tends, over time, to build the courts and competitive pressures that suppress clientelism and corruption, so democracy shapes neopatrimonialism as much as the reverse (reverse causality, or simultaneity when the two move together). A one-year lag guards against the most immediate version of this but not the slower feedback, since both series are highly persistent.
Therefore, neopatrimonialism acts here as a control, holding the institutional context fixed while we ask about oil – not as a quantity whose coefficient you should report as “the effect of neopatrimonialism on democratic survival.”

title: Part II: Markov Transition Models with Correlated Random Effects
text:
Exercise 4: Report it (Results Table)
Produce a single modelsummary table presenting, for the modernisation exercise, the static probit, the LDV probit, and the two CRE MTM models side by side, with the AUCs as a custom row and cluster-robust standard errors throughout.

library(modelsummary)
library(tinytable)
library(sandwich)
library(tibble)

# Cluster-robust vcovs. Static and LDV use the plain probits; the MTM columns
# use the CRE specifications. All clustered by country.
vcov_list <- list(
  "Cluster-Robust" = vcovCL(probit_1,        cluster = ~ countrycode, type = "HC3"),
  "Cluster-Robust" = vcovCL(probit_ldv,      cluster = ~ countrycode, type = "HC3"),
  "Cluster-Robust" = vcovCL(emergence_1_cre, cluster = ~ countrycode, type = "HC3"),
  "Cluster-Robust" = vcovCL(survival_1_cre,  cluster = ~ countrycode, type = "HC3")
)

models_ex1 <- list(
  "Static"    = probit_1,
  "LDV"       = probit_ldv,
  "Emergence" = emergence_1_cre,
  "Survival"  = survival_1_cre
)

# The mean_ (CRE) terms are left out of coef_map: dropped from display while
# still controlling the estimates.
cm <- c(
  "l.log_gdppc"    = "Log GDP pc (lagged)",
  "l.gdppc_growth" = "GDP growth (lagged)",
  "l.democracy"    = "Democracy (lagged)",
  "(Intercept)"    = "(Intercept)"
)

rows <- tibble(
  `~term` = "AUC",
  `~(1)`  = as.numeric(auc(roc_p1)),
  `~(2)`  = as.numeric(auc(roc_ldv)),
  `~(3)`  = as.numeric(auc(roc_em1)),
  `~(4)`  = as.numeric(auc(roc_sur1))
)
attr(rows, "position") <- 9

modelsummary(
  models_ex1,
  vcov      = vcov_list,
  estimate  = "{estimate}{stars}",
  statistic = "({std.error})",
  gof_omit  = "DF|Deviance|Log.Lik|F|AIC|BIC|RMSE",
  coef_map  = cm,
  add_rows  = rows,
  notes     = c(
    "+ p < 0.1, * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001",
    "Standard errors are cluster-robust (HC3), clustered by country.",
    "Emergence and Survival columns include country means (Correlated Random Effects), omitted from the table; Static and LDV do not."
  )
) |>
  group_tt(j = list("MTM" = 4:5)) |>
  group_tt(j = list("Dependent Variable: Democracy" = 2:5))|>
  theme_latex(resize_width= 0.75, resize_direction="both")


What this table is doing. The vcov argument feeds in the cluster-robust matrices, so the standard errors in parentheses are the corrected ones. The Emergence and Survival columns are the CRE specifications, carrying the country means as hidden controls – which is why the note flags that the MTM columns differ from Static and LDV. And statistic = "({std.error})" makes explicit that it is the standard error in parentheses, the convention in comparative politics.


Reflection Questions

Read l.log_gdppc across the four columns. It shrinks from the static probit to the LDV probit, then splits in the MTM columns – weak for emergence, sizeable for survival. Two things change at once as you enter the MTM columns: the conditioning on last year’s regime and the addition of the country means. With that in mind, what does the whole progression tell you about how path dependence and unobserved heterogeneity together shape the modernisation result?
The emergence and survival AUCs are not comparable with the static and LDV ones (different subsets), but compare the two MTM columns with each other. Which model fits its own data better, and why is a high survival AUC less impressive than a respectable emergence AUC?
Column 2 forces a single l.democracy coefficient to stand in for both transition processes at once. Given what Exercises 1 to 3 showed about how differently emergence and survival behave, explain why that is a poor approximation and what substantive information it hides.

title: Part II: Markov Transition Models with Correlated Random Effects
text:
Synthesis Questions

Across all three theories, do the variables that predict democratic emergence also predict democratic survival, or are the two processes driven by different things? Use your CRE MTM coefficients – and, where it matters, the distinction between the within-country lagged terms and the between-country means – to support your answer.
You have now seen two ways of bringing time into a binary-outcome model: the probit with a lagged dependent variable, and the Markov Transition Model. In two or three sentences, state the key substantive difference between them and why the MTM is the more appropriate choice for studying regime transitions.
Throughout, democracy has been measured as a binary. Reflect briefly on what is gained and lost by treating it as a threshold rather than a continuous measure of democratic quality – and say which process, emergence or survival, you think is the more distorted by the binary coding, and why.
Step 3b added the country means (CRE) to guard against unobserved heterogeneity; Step 4 clustered the standard errors. In your own words, what distinct problem does each correction solve, and why do you need both rather than just one?

title: Full Glossary
text:
Full Glossary



Unless otherwise noted, the definitions are taken from Linke (forthcoming).



 



Adjusted R-Squared


A version of R\(^2\) that adjusts for the number of independent variables in a multiple regression, providing a more unbiased estimate of the proportion of variance explained




analysis


A detailed evaluation of data to discover their structure and relevant information to answer a research question




area under the curve (AUC)


A scalar summary of the ROC curve, equal to the area beneath it and bounded between 0 and 1. An AUC of 1 indicates perfect classification, an AUC of 0.5 indicates no predictive power (equivalent to random guessing), and an AUC below 0.5 indicates a model that systematically predicts the wrong category. AUC values are particularly useful for comparing the fit of competing models on the same data.




asymmetry


The notion that while X causes Y, Y does not cause X. It is established with temporal priority, manipulated events, and/or the independence of causes




attribute


A component or characteristic of a concept




autocorrelation (of error terms)


Autocorrelation occurs when the values of error terms are correlated across observations. No autocorrelation implies that the covariance between error terms is zero




autocorrelation


Autocorrelation occurs when the values of error terms are correlated across observations. No autocorrelation implies that the covariance between error terms is zero




autocorrelation (of error terms)


Autocorrelation occurs when the values of error terms are correlated across observations. No autocorrelation implies that the covariance between error terms is zero




background concept


The broad constellation of meanings and understandings associated with the concept




categorical


Describing the qualitative categories of a characteristic, for example different religions




causal loop


Y causes itself (e.g., health; happiness, wealth)




causality


In order to establish a causal relationship, the following criteria must be met concurrently:

Relevance of the variables within the broader theoretical and empirical context of the research

Empirical Context
Clear Theoretical Framework
Clear Conceptualization
Exclusion of alternative explanations

Asymmetry
Significant (and sufficiently strong) statistical association





ceteris paribus


A Latin phrase meaning “all other things being equal”. In statistics and econometrics, a ceteris paribus interpretation describes the effect of changing one independent variable on the outcome variable while holding all other variables in the model constant.




cluster-robust standard errors


Standard errors adjusted to account for the fact that observations within the same group (cluster) are correlated with one another, whilst assuming independence across groups. In panel data, countries typically serve as clusters, since repeated observations on the same country are unlikely to be independent over time. Cluster-robust standard errors are generally larger and more conservative than default standard errors, reflecting the reduced effective information content of correlated observations.




coefficient


In a regression model or equation, a coefficient is a numerical expression which is multiplied with the value of a variable




concept


Abstract ideas which form the building blocks of theories




conceptualisation


Formulating a systematized concept through reasoning about the background concept, in light of the goals of research




conditional probability


The probability of an event occurring given that another event has already occurred, written \(P(A\mid B)\), where the vertical bar is read as “given”. In a Markov Transition Model, the conditional probability \(P(y_{i,t} = 1 \mid y_{i,t-1} = 0)\) expresses the probability of a country being a democracy in year \(t\), given that it was an autocracy in year \(t-1\).




confidence interval


A confidence interval is an estimated range, based on a sample, that is likely to contain the true population parameter (such as the mean). If the sampling process were repeated many times, approximately \((1 - \alpha) \times 100%\) of the resulting intervals would contain the true parameter. The value of ( ) determines the confidence level – for example, \(\alpha = 0.05\) corresponds to a 95% confidence level, while \(\alpha = 0.01\) corresponds to 99%




confidence level


The confidence level is the proportion of confidence intervals, constructed from repeated random samples of the same population using the same method, that are expected to contain the true population parameter. It is denoted by ( 1 - ), where ( ) is the significance level. For example, a 95% confidence level implies that 95% of such intervals would contain the true parameter in the long run




construct overlap


A situation in which the independent and dependent variables partly measure the same underlying concept, so that their association is partly definitional rather than causal. Because the overlap lies in what the variables measure rather than in the error term, it is distinct from endogeneity and cannot be removed by any choice of model, lag, fixed effect, or instrument; the remedy lies in conceptualisation and measurement.




continuous


Can assume any value within defined measurement boundaries




control variable


A variable that is held constant or included in a statistical model to account for its potential influence, allowing clearer estimation of the relationship between the main independent and dependent variables




Correlated Random Effects


A method for estimating panel data models that allows the unobserved individual-specific effects to be correlated with the explanatory variables. The correlated random effects (CRE) approach, also known as the Mundlak approach, models this correlation by including the individual-specific means of the time-varying explanatory variables as additional regressors. This produces coefficient estimates for the time-varying variables that are equivalent to those from a fixed-effects model, while also allowing the effects of time-invariant variables to be estimated.




correlation


A standardised measure of the linear relationship between two variables (\(x_i\) and \(y_i\)), bounded between \(-1\) and \(1\), which indicates both the direction and strength of their association.




correlation


A standardised measure of the linear relationship between two variables (\(x_i\) and \(y_i\)), bounded between \(-1\) and \(1\), which indicates both the direction and strength of their association.




covariance


A measure which assesses the degree to which the values of two variables (\(x_i\) and \(y_i\)) vary together (their joint variability).




critical t-value


A critical t-value, \(t_{\text{crit}}\), is a threshold value from the t-distribution with \(n - 1\) degrees of freedom that defines the boundaries of a confidence interval. For a \((1 - \alpha)\) confidence interval, \(t_{\text{crit}}\) is the value such that: \[P(-t_{\text{crit}} \leq t \leq t_{\text{crit}}) = 1 - \alpha\] where \(1 - \alpha\) is the confidence level




cross-sectional data


Look at different units (or cross-sections) \(i\) at a single point in time




cumulative distribution function (CDF)


The cumulative distribution function (CDF) describes how probability accumulates up to a given value. It gives the probability that a random variable \(X\) is less than or equal to a specified value \(x\), that is, \(F(x)=P(X\leq x)\). As \(x\) moves from the smallest to the largest possible value, the CDF increases from 0 to 1. For continuous random variables, the CDF is obtained by integrating the probability density function (PDF).




data


Derives from the Latin “datum” which means “given”. For our purposes it is a collection of information or numbers (or quantities) for the purpose of analysis




data set


A collection of numerical values for individual observations, separated into distinctive variables




degrees of freedom


Degrees of freedom express constraints on our estimation process by specifying how many values in the calculation are free to vary




dependent variable


Is dependent through some statistical or stochastic process on the value of an independent variable




descriptive statistics


Summarise information about the centre and variability of a variable




dichotomous


Can only assume two mutually exclusive, but internally homogeneous qualitative categories




discrete


The result of a counting process




discussion


The purpose of the discussion section in a research project is to interpret the results, explain their implications, compare them with existing literature, and highlight their significance, limitations, and potential for future research




endogeneity


A situation in which an explanatory variable is correlated with the error term of a model (with influences on the outcome that the model does not capture). This biases the estimated effect of the variable, because part of what is attributed to it in fact originates elsewhere. Endogeneity commonly arises from omitted (confounding) variables, reverse causality or simultaneity, or measurement error in the explanatory variable




error term


The error term quantifies the distance between each observation and the corresponding point on the regression line. The terms are denoted as \(\epsilon_{i}\)




False Positive Rate (FPR)


The proportion of actual negative cases that are incorrectly predicted as positive. It is calculated as \(\text{FPR} = \frac{\text{FP}}{\text{FP} + \text{TN}}\), where FP denotes false positives and TN denotes true negatives. The false positive rate is plotted on the horizontal axis of the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve.




Fixed Effects Model


A panel data model that controls for unobserved, time-invariant heterogeneity across units by allowing each unit to have its own intercept, so that parameters are identified from within-unit variation rather than from differences across units.




generalised linear model


A family of models which allows us to estimate a linear relationship between dependent and independent variables even though the underlying relationship is not linear by means of a link function. It also allows us to vary the assumed distribution of our error terms




heteroscedasticity


The variability of the error terms changes for different observations \(X\)




hypothesis


In statistics, a hypothesis is a formal statement about a population parameter or relationship between variables. Hypotheses guide statistical tests to determine whether data support or refute them. The hypothesis suggesting an effect or difference is called the alternative hypothesis. The alternative hypothesis is always paired with a null-hypothesis, suggesting no effect or difference.




incidental parameters problem


A problem that arises in statistical models when the number of parameters increases with the sample size. In panel data models with fixed effects, for example, each individual may have its own parameter, so the number of parameters grows as more individuals are observed. As a result, estimates of the parameters of primary interest may remain biased or inconsistent, even when the number of observations becomes large. The incidental parameters problem is especially important in nonlinear models, such as fixed-effects logit or probit models, where standard estimation methods may not produce consistent estimates.




independent variable


Influences or helps us predict the level of a dependent variable. It is often treated as fixed, or “given” in statistical analysis, and is sometimes also called “explanatory variable”




interaction effect


An interaction effect occurs when the effect of one independent variable, \(x_1\), on a dependent variable, \(y\), depends on the level of another independent variable, \(x_2\). In other words, the impact of \(x_1\) on \(y\) is not constant but varies depending on the value of \(x_2\), indicating that the two variables jointly influence the outcome in a non-additive way




intercept


The intercept is the point at which the regression line intersects the y-axis. In this book we denote it as \(\beta_{0}\)




latent variable


Variables that can only be inferred indirectly through a mathematical model from other observable variables that can be directly observed or measured




listwise deletion


When a value within an observation is missing, the entire observation is dropped




literature review


An analytical summary of the literature relating to a particular topic with the objective of identifying a gap and thus motivating a research question




logarithm


Logarithm is defined as the exponent or power to which a base must be raised to yield a given number. Expressed mathematically, \(x\) is the logarithm of \(n\) to the base \(b\) if \(b^x = n\), in which case \(x = log_b n\)




marginal effect


A marginal effect is the change in the predicted probability of the outcome for a one-unit change in a predictor




Markov Transition Model


A model which estimates the probability of being in a given state at time \(t\), conditional on the state occupied in the previous period \(t-1\). In the context of democratisation, this means modelling the probability of a country being a democracy this year given its regime type in the previous year, allowing emergence and survival to be estimated as separate conditional processes.




mean


Is equal to the sum of the observations divided by the number of observations




measurement


Refers to the selection of a measure or variable




median


Separates the lower half from the upper half of observations




method


A tool for systematic investigation




mode


Is the most frequently occurring value




model building


Running a number of regression models, each testing a different combination of variables




moderator


A moderator is a variable that conditions how a predictor is related to an outcome. In other words, it tells us whether the predictor’s association with the outcome is stronger, weaker, or different under particular values of the moderator




multi causality


Multicausality refers to a situation in which an outcome variable \(y\) is influenced by multiple independent variables, such that \(x_1\), \(x_2\), \(x_3\), all contribute to explaining variations in \(y\). In this context, no single variable fully accounts for changes in \(y\); instead, the outcome is the result of the combined effects of several causes. We distinguish a speacial case here in which the independent variables are interdependent




N


The number of observations under investigation




normal distribution


The normal distribution is a bell-shaped probability distribution that is symmetrical around the mean. Approximately 68% of values fall within 1 standard deviation of the mean, 95.4% within 2 standard deviations, and 99.7% within 3 standard deviations. This is known as the empirical rule.




Null-Hypothesis Significance Testing


A test of statistical significance is a procedure for assessing whether observed data are consistent with a specified null hypothesis, which usually asserts no effect, difference, or relationship. By evaluating how likely the data are under this assumption, we can decide whether to reject the null. Because it centers on testing the null hypothesis, this method is called null-hypothesis significance testing (NHST).




observed t-value


The observed t-value is a standardised test statistic that measures how many standard errors a sample statistic (typically a sample mean) lies from a hypothesised population parameter: \[\frac{\bar{y} - \mu_{0}}{se}, \quad\quad \text{where} \quad se = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\] where \(\bar{y}\) is the sample mean, \(\mu_0\) is the hypothesised population mean, \(s\) is the sample standard deviation, and \(n\) is the sample size. Because the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is unknown and estimated from the data, the t-score follows a t-distribution with \(n - 1\) degrees of freedom rather than a standard normal distribution




omitted variable bias


If you omit an important variable in a regression model, it will bias the size of other coefficients if the variables are correlated.




omitted variable bias


If you omit an important variable in a regression model, it will bias the size of other coefficients if the variables are correlated.




Ordinary Least Squares


The method of fitting a regression line by means of minimizing the sum of the squared distances between the observations and the estimated values




parameter


A parameter is a fixed value that characterizes a population, such as the population mean or variance




parsimony


Refers to the principle “as many as necessary, as few as possible”




partial slope coefficient


A partial slope coefficient measures the influence of a variable in multiple regression, holding all other independent variables in the model constant




polynomial


A polynomial is a function of a variable \(x\) that can be written as a finite sum of powers of \(x\) multiplied by coefficients, for example \[
	y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2 + \cdots + \beta_k x^k,
	\] where \(k\) is a non-negative integer and the coefficients \(\beta_0, \beta_1, \ldots, \beta_k\) are fixed constants.




pooling


The combining of observations across multiple units and time periods into a single dataset. A pooled OLS estimator treats all observations as independent and does not account for unobserved heterogeneity across units, which can lead to biased and inconsistent estimates if such heterogeneity is present. Furthermore, observations within the same unit are likely correlated across time, violating the assumption of independent errors and necessitating the use of cluster-robust standard errors.




population


Collection of all cases which possess certain pre-defined characteristics




Population Regression Function


The Population Regression Function (PRF) describes the expected distribution of \(y\), given the values of the independent variable(s) \(x\). It is also called the conditional expectation function (CEF) and can be denoted as \(E(y_{i}|x_{i})\)




predicted probabilities


The value of a predicted probability is equal to the cumulative density function, \(F(X^\prime\beta)\), evaluated at a chosen value of the independent variable




probability


Refers to how many times out of a total number of cases a particular event occurs. We can also see it as the chance of a particular event occurring




probability distribution


Specifies the likelihood of all possible outcomes for a particular variable




p-value


The p-value indicates the probability of observing a test statistic at least as extreme as the one actually observed in the direction of the alternative hypothesis, assuming the null hypothesis is true. Common thresholds for significance are 0.05, 0.01, and 0.001. A smaller p-value suggests stronger evidence against the null hypothesis. The p-value is denoted as \(p\).




quartile


Divides ordered data into four equal parts and indicates the percentage of observations that falls into the respective quartile and below




Coefficient of Determination


States the proportion of the variation of the dependent variable which is explained through the model. It is defined as \(\frac{\text{Explained Sum of Squares}}{\text{Total Sum of Squares}}\)




range


The difference between the largest and the smallest observation




regression line


The regression line describes how the dependent variable is functionally related to the values of the independent variable. It it defined by the intercept \(\beta_{0}\) and the slope \(\beta_{1}\)




research question


A specific enquiry relating to a particular topic or subject. It forms the starting point of the research cycle




residual


An estimation of the error term. The difference between an observation \(y_{i}\) and the estimated value \(\hat{y}_{i}\). Denoted as \(\hat{\epsilon}_{i}\)




reverse causality


Causality runs from x to y. If y could also cause x, then we deal with reverse causality.




ROC curve


A graphical measure of model fit for binary outcome models, constructed by plotting the True Positive Rate (TPR) against the False Positive Rate (FPR) across all possible classification thresholds \(\tau\). A model with no predictive power traces the diagonal where TPR \(=\) FPR, whilst a model with perfect separation produces a curve reaching the upper-left corner. The further the curve lies above the diagonal, the better the model distinguishes between the two categories of the dependent variable.




sample


A sub-group of the population




Sample Regression Function


A regression line based on a randomly drawn sample




secondary data


Secondary data are data which have been collected by somebody else




significance level


The significance level, denoted by \(\alpha\), is the threshold used in hypothesis testing to determine if a result is statistically significant. It represents the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis even though it is actually true (a Type I error). Common levels are 0.05 or 0.01, indicating 5% or 1% risk.




simultaneity


Simultaneity (or bidirectional causation) occurs when \(x\) and \(y\) influence each other at the same time, so that both \(x \rightarrow y\) and \(y \rightarrow x\) hold and neither variable is purely exogenous.




slope


A slope is defined as rise over run, and so it tells us how many units of y we need to climb (or descend if the slope is negative) for every additional unit of the independent variable \(x\)




Social Sciences


Are concerned with the study of society and seek to scientifically describe and explain the behaviour of actors




standard deviation


The standard deviation s is defined as \[\begin{equation*}
			s=\sqrt{\frac{\text{sum of squared deviations}}{\text{sample size} -1}}=\sqrt{\frac{\Sigma(y_{i} - \bar{y})^2}{n-1}}
			\end{equation*}\]quation*}




standard error


The standard deviation of the sampling distribution. It is defined as: \[\begin{equation}
	\sigma_{\bar{y}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
	\end{equation}\]on}




symmetry


In the context of causation, symmetry is understood as the law-like regularity of events. There needs to be a recipe (causal mechanism) which regularly produces effects from causes




systematized concept


A specific formulation of a concept used by a given scholar or group of scholars; commonly involves an explicit definition




t-distribution


The t-Distribution is bell-shaped and symmetrical around a mean of zero. Its shape is dependent on the degrees of freedom in the estimation process




theory


A formal set of ideas that is intended to explain why something happens or exists (Oxford Learner’s Dictionaries)




time-series data


Time-series data review a certain characteristic over time \(t\), where \(t\) runs from 1 to \(T\)




true and false positives and negatives


The four possible outcomes when comparing a model’s predicted classification against the observed outcome. A true positive (TP) occurs when the model correctly predicts a positive outcome (e.g. democracy); a true negative (TN) when it correctly predicts a negative outcome (e.g. dictatorship); a false positive (FP) when it predicts a positive outcome that is not observed; and a false negative (FN) when it predicts a negative outcome for a case that is in fact positive.




True Positive Rate (TPR)


The proportion of actual positive cases that are correctly predicted as positive, also known as sensitivity. It is calculated as \(\text{TPR} = \frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP} + \text{FN}}\), where TP denotes true positives and FN denotes false negatives. The true positive rate is plotted on the vertical axis of the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve.




true positive rate and false positive rate


Summary statistics derived from a confusion matrix. The true positive rate (TPR, also called sensitivity) is the proportion of actual positive cases correctly predicted as positive: \(\text{TPR} = \frac{\text{TP}}{\text{TP} + \text{FN}}\). The false positive rate (FPR) is the proportion of actual negative cases incorrectly predicted as positive: \(\text{FPR} = \frac{\text{FP}}{\text{FP} + \text{TN}}\). These two rates are plotted against one another across all thresholds to produce the ROC curve.




time-series, cross sectional (TSCS) data


Time-series, cross-sectional data look at different units \(i\) across time \(t\)




Unobserved Heterogeneity


Differences across units of observation that affect the outcome of interest but are not captured by the observed explanatory variables, becoming absorbed into the error term and potentially biasing estimates when correlated with the regressors.




Unobserved Heterogeneity


Differences across units of observation that affect the outcome of interest but are not captured by the observed explanatory variables, becoming absorbed into the error term and potentially biasing estimates when correlated with the regressors.




variable


An element of a conceptual component which varies. We also call these “measures”




variance


Is equal to the squared standard deviation




Variance Inflation Factor


A measure to quantify the how much larger the observed variance of a coefficient is compared to a scenario in which the variable was totally functionally independent from the other independent variables in the model




Variance-Covariance Matrix


A variance-covariance is a square matrix that encapsulates the variances of different variables on its diagonal and the covariances between pairs of variables in its off-diagonal elements.




Variance-Covariance Matrix


A variance-covariance is a square matrix that encapsulates the variances of different variables on its diagonal and the covariances between pairs of variables in its off-diagonal elements.




year fixed effects


Indicator variables for each time period included in a regression model, which absorb everything that affected all units simultaneously in a given year. In cross-national panel data, year fixed effects account for global shocks — such as the end of the Cold War or the 2008 financial crisis — that introduce contemporaneous correlation across countries. Their inclusion is a design choice rather than a default: if they are not jointly significant, they add no explanatory power, and in binary outcome models with rare events they can cause complete separation, producing unreliable estimates.
